Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 1–4 (part 1 of 2):

Page 122
(Surat ash-Shura)
Fifty-three verses, Meccan
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Ha-Mim﴾ ﴿’Ayn-Sin-Qaf﴾ ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, God, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them, and the angels glorify their Lord with praise and ask forgiveness for those on the earth. Surely God is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿As for those who take protectors other than Him, God is watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾

God Most High says: ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ ﴿’Ayn-Sin-Qaf﴾ ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, God, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾ ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them, and the angels glorify their Lord with praise and ask forgiveness for those on the earth. Surely God is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿As for those who take protectors other than Him, God is watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾

Know that discussion of openings like these is well known. However, at this point there are two additional questions. The first: it may be asked, since these seven surahs all begin with His saying ﴿Ha-Mim﴾, what is the reason for this surah's being singled out with the addition of ﴿’Ayn-Sin-Qaf﴾?
The second: they agreed that there is no separation between ﴿Kaf-Ha-Ya-’Ayn-Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1], but here a separation is made between ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ and ﴿’Ayn-Sin-Qaf﴾. What is the reason for this?

Know that discussion of openings like these is narrow, and opening the door to conjecture is something with no path to it. So it is better to entrust their knowledge to God. Ibn ‘Abbas and Ibn Mas‘ud recited ﴿Ha-Mim ’Ayn-Sin-Qaf﴾.

As for His saying ﴿Thus does He reveal to you﴾, the kaf means "like," and dha is used to point to something previously mentioned. So the meaning is: like ﴿Ha-Mim﴾ ﴿’Ayn-Sin-Qaf﴾ ﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you﴾. From this two opinions arise:
Page 123
The first: it is reported from Ibn ‘Abbas, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "There has not been a prophet who was a possessor of a scripture except that ﴿Ha-Mim ’Ayn-Sin-Qaf﴾ was revealed to him." This, in my view, is far-fetched.

The second: the meaning is: like the Book named "Ha-Mim ’Ayn-Sin-Qaf," God reveals to you and to those before you. The likeness intended here is the likeness in calling to monotheism, justice, prophethood, and the return (ma‘ad), and in censuring the state of this world and encouraging orientation toward the Hereafter. What confirms this is that we have explained in the surah ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A‘la: 1] that its beginning is in establishing monotheism, its middle in establishing prophethood, and its end in establishing the return. When it completed the discussion establishing these three matters, He said: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A‘la: 18–19]. He means that the purpose of sending down all the divine books is nothing but these three matters. Likewise here: like the Book named "Ha-Mim ’Ayn-Sin-Qaf," God reveals to you and to every prophet before you. The likeness intended by this is the call to these lofty matters and sacred divine subjects. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "He did not say 'revealed to you' but said ﴿reveals to you﴾ in the present tense, to indicate that the revelation of the like of it is His custom."

Ibn Kathir recited ﴿Thus is revealed﴾ with a fatha on the ha, in the passive form, which is one of the two transmissions from Abu ‘Amr; and some recited ﴿Nuhi﴾ with a nun. The rest recited ﴿reveals to you and to those before you﴾ with a kasra on the ha.

If it is asked: on the first reading, what is the subject (rafi‘) of the name of God, Exalted? We say: what is indicated by the revelation (wahy), as if someone asked, "Who is the revealer?" and it was said, "God." A parallel to this is the reading of al-Sulami: ﴿And thus their partners have made to seem fair the killing of their children to many of the polytheists﴾ [al-An‘am: 137], in the passive form, with ﴿their partners﴾ in the nominative. If it is asked, what is the subject in the case of one who reads ﴿Nuhi﴾ with a nun? We say it is in the nominative by being the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada’), and "al-‘Aziz" and what follows are predicates; or ﴿al-‘Aziz al-Hakim﴾ are two attributes, and the adverbial phrase is its predicate. Since He mentioned that this Book came about through revelation, He clarified who the Revealer is, so He said that He is the Mighty, the Wise. We have explained at the beginning of the surah "Ha-Mim, the Believer" that His being Mighty indicates His being capable of what has no end, and His being Wise indicates His being knowing of all that is known and free of need of all needs. Thus from His being Mighty and Wise there results for us that He is capable of all that is capable, knowing of all that is known, free of all needs. And whoever is like this, his actions and sayings are wisdom and correctness, and are free of defect and purposelessness. The author of this book said: I have said in a qasida:

All praise belongs to God, Lord of bounties and favors, of grace, generosity, benevolence and nobility,
Whose act is exalted above defect and purposelessness, whose dominion is sanctified above deposition and non-existence.

The third attribute is His saying ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, and this indicates two matters of utmost majesty. The first: that He is described as having complete, pervasive power over all parts of the heavens and the earth, despite their greatness and vastness, through bringing into being and annihilating, through creating and nullifying.

The second: that since He made clear by His saying ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ that everything in the heavens and on the earth is His possession and property, it must be that He is exalted above being located within the heavens or within the earth, for otherwise He would be a possession of Himself.

And if it is established that He is not in any of the heavens, it is impossible for Him to be in the Throne either; for everything that is above you is a heaven, so if the Throne exists above the heavens, it is in reality a heaven. Therefore whatever is located in the Throne must be God's possession and property, so He must be exalted above being located in the Throne. If they say: God, Exalted, said ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾, and the word "what" (ma) includes those who have reason, we say: this is rebutted in two ways. The first:
Page 124
the word "ma" occurs regarding God, Exalted: He said ﴿By the heaven and He who built it, by the earth and He who spread it out﴾ [al-Shams: 5–6], and He said ﴿I do not worship what you worship, nor are you worshippers of what I worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 2–3].

The second: the form "man" (who) occurs in a surah like this, as He said: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but he comes to the Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]. The word "man" undoubtedly occurs regarding God, Exalted, so this verse indicates that everyone in the heavens and the earth is a servant of God. So if God were existing in the heavens and the earth and in the Throne, He would be among those in the heavens, and therefore He would be a servant of God. Since this verse establishes that everyone existing in the heavens and the Throne is a servant of God, it is necessary that He whose greatness is sanctified above the accusation of servitude be exalted above being located in place, direction, the Throne, and the Footstool.

The fourth and fifth attributes: His saying, ﴿and He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾. It is not permissible for His being "Most High" to mean highness in direction or place, since the proof of its invalidity has been established; nor is it permissible for "the Mighty" to mean greatness of body and largeness of frame, for that would entail His being composed of parts and components, and that is contrary to His saying ﴿God is One﴾. Therefore "the Most High" must mean one exalted above resemblance to contingent things and fitness with created things, and "the Mighty" must mean greatness in power, dominance through exaltedness, and the perfection of divinity.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them﴾, and in this there are issues:

First issue: Abu ‘Amr and ‘Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read ﴿takadu﴾ with a ta, ﴿yanfatirna﴾ with a ya and a nun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn ‘Amir, Hafs from ‘Asim, and Hamza read ﴿takadu﴾ with a ta, ﴿yatafattarna﴾ with a ya and a ta. Nafi‘ and al-Kisa’i read ﴿yakadu﴾ with a ya, ﴿yatafattarna﴾ also with a ta. The author of al-Kashshaf said: Yunus reported from Abu ‘Amr an unusual reading, ﴿tatafattarna﴾ with two tas and a nun, and a rare parallel to it is reported in the Nawadir of Ibn al-A‘rabi: "al-ibilu tatashammasna" (the camels bask in the sun).

Second issue: concerning the benefit of His saying ﴿yatafattarna min fawqihinna﴾, there are several views:

The first: ‘Ikrima reported from Ibn ‘Abbas that he said regarding ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them﴾: the meaning is that they nearly split from the weight of God upon them.

Know that this view is feeble, and one must firmly declare Ibn ‘Abbas innocent of it. Several points show its invalidity. The first: His saying ﴿from above them﴾ is not understood as "from those above them." Second: grant that it is taken that way; but why do you say that this state arose from God's weight upon them? Why is it not permissible to say that this state arose from the weight of the angels upon them, as has come in the hadith that he, ﷺ, said: "The heaven groaned, and it has the right to groan: there is not a space the width of a hand in it but that there is an angel standing, or bowing, or prostrating." Third: why is it not permissible that the meaning is: the heavens nearly break and split from awe of One who is above them, above in divinity, dominance and power? By these points it is established that the view they have mentioned is utterly corrupt and feeble.

The second way of interpreting the verse is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned: that the word of disbelief came from those beneath the heavens, and the analogy would have been to say "yatafattarna min tahtihinna" (split from beneath them) from the direction from which the word came; but it was exaggerated, so it was reversed and made to have an effect in the direction of above, as if it were said: "they nearly split from the direction that is above them," leaving aside the direction beneath them. A parallel to this exaggeration is His saying: ﴿Boiling water is poured over their heads﴾ ﴿whereby what is in their bellies and their skins are melted﴾ [al-Hajj: 19–20], where it is made to have an effect on their inner parts.

The third way of interpreting the verse: ﴿min fawqihinna﴾ means "from above the earths," because before this verse He said ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, then said:
Page 125
﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them﴾, that is, from above the earths.

The fourth way of interpretation: the meaning of ﴿min fawqihinna﴾ is from the direction in which these heavens are located, and that direction is "above"; so His saying ﴿min fawqihinna﴾ means from the upper direction in which they are.

Third issue: they differed over why this condition arose. There are two views. The first: when He made clear that the One who revealed this Book is God, the Mighty, the Wise, He described His majesty and grandeur, saying ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them﴾, that is, from His awe and majesty. The second view: the cause of their attributing a son to God is His saying ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it﴾; and here the cause is their attributing partners to God, as indicated by His saying after this verse: ﴿As for those who take protectors other than Him﴾. The correct view is the first. Then He said: ﴿The angels glorify their Lord with praise and ask forgiveness for those on the earth﴾.

Know that God's created beings are of two kinds: the corporeal world (al-Jismaniyyat), the greatest of which are the heavens, and the spiritual world (al-Ruhaniyyat), the greatest of which are the angels. God establishes the perfection of His greatness in order to show the reach of His power and the awe of His majesty over corporeal beings. Then He follows this with the reach of His power and the dominance of His awe over spiritual beings. The evidence for this is that in the surah of ﴿They ask one another﴾ [al-Naba: 1], when He wished to establish greatness and majesty, He began with mention of corporeal beings, saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Most Merciful, none have the power to address Him﴾ [al-Naba: 37]. Then He moved to mention the spiritual world, saying: ﴿On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and who says what is right﴾ [al-Naba: 38]. Likewise, in this verse, He demonstrates the perfection of His greatness by the dominance of His awe over corporeal beings, saying: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them﴾. Then He moved to mention the spiritual beings, saying: ﴿And the angels glorify their Lord with praise﴾. This is a noble arrangement and a striking exposition.

Know that existent beings are of three categories: an agent that is not acted upon, which is God, glorified and exalted, and it is the most noble of the categories; a thing that is acted upon and does not act, which is the receptive, namely body (al-Jism), and it is the lowliest of the categories; and an existent that receives influence from the first category and exerts influence on the second, which is the sanctified spiritual substances (al-Jawahir al-Ruhaniyyat), and it is the intermediate rank.

Having understood this, we say: spiritual substances have two relations. One is a relation to the world of majesty and greatness, which is the relation of receptivity, for when the holy emanations and the eternal lights shine upon spiritual substances, their substances are illumined and their quiddities are radiant.

Then, when spiritual substances have derived those spiritual powers, they become strong enough through them to dominate the worlds of corporeal beings. Since this is so, they have two faces: a face toward the side of greatness and the presence of majesty, and a face toward the world of bodies. The first face is more noble than the second. Having understood this, we say:

Then He follows this with the reach of His power and the dominance of His awe over spiritual beings. The evidence for this is that in the surah of ﴿They ask one another﴾ [al-Naba: 1], when He wished to establish greatness and majesty, He began with mention of corporeal beings, saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Most Merciful, none have the power to address Him﴾ [al-Naba: 37]. Then He moved to mention the spiritual world, saying: ﴿On the day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and who says what is right﴾ [al-Naba: 38]. Likewise, in this verse, He demonstrates the perfection of His greatness by the dominance of His awe over corporeal beings, saying: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from above them﴾. Then He moved to mention the spiritual beings, saying: ﴿And the angels glorify their Lord with praise﴾. This is a noble arrangement and a striking exposition.

Know that existent beings are of three categories: an agent that is not acted upon, which is God, glorified and exalted, and it is the most noble of the categories; a thing that is acted upon and does not act, which is the receptive, namely body (al-Jism), and it is the lowliest of the categories; and an existent that receives influence from the first category and exerts influence on the second, which is the sanctified spiritual substances (al-Jawahir al-Ruhaniyyat), and it is the intermediate rank.

Having understood this, we say: spiritual substances have two relations. One is a relation to the world of majesty and greatness, which is the relation of receptivity, for when the holy emanations and the eternal lights shine upon spiritual substances, their substances are illumined and their quiddities are radiant.

Then, when spiritual substances have derived those spiritual powers, they become strong enough through them to dominate the worlds of corporeal beings. Since this is so, they have two faces: a face toward the side of greatness and the presence of majesty, and a face toward the world of bodies. The first face is more noble than the second. Having understood this, we say:

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 5–6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They glorify their Lord with His praise﴾, is an indication of the aspect they have toward the world of majesty and grandeur. His saying: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those on earth﴾, is an indication of the aspect they have toward the world of bodies. How beautiful are these subtleties, how noble they are, and how strongly they affect the drawing of souls from the lowest of creation to the summit of knowledge of the Truth. Having understood this, we say: As for the first aspect, which is the exalted and sanctified aspect, it includes two matters. The first is glorification (tasbih), and the second is praise (tahmid). His saying, ﴿They glorify their Lord with His praise﴾, conveys these two matters. Glorification precedes praise, because glorification is an expression of exalting God, Exalted is He, above what is not fitting, while praise is an expression of describing Him as the one who bestows every good. His being transcendent in His essence above what is not fitting takes precedence in rank over His being the overflowing giver of goods and blessings, because the existence of a thing takes precedence over its bringing other things into being, and its being established in itself takes precedence over its effect in the establishment of others. For this reason glorification precedes praise, and for this reason He said: ﴿They glorify their Lord with His praise﴾.

As for the second aspect, which is the aspect those souls have toward the world of corporeal things, it is indicated by His saying: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those on earth﴾. What is meant by it is their effects on the ordering of the affairs of this world and the attainment therein of the most correct and most beneficial path. These are glimpses of lofty divine investigations embedded in these sacred verses. Let us return to what befits the science of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis). If it is said: How is it valid that they seek forgiveness for those on earth when among them are the unbelievers, and He, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿Upon them is the curse of God and the angels﴾? How then can they be cursing them and also seeking forgiveness for them? We say, the answer to this is from several aspects:

The first: His saying, ﴿for those on earth﴾, does not convey generality, because it is valid to say that they sought forgiveness for everyone on earth, and it is also valid to say that they sought forgiveness for some of those on earth and not others. Had His saying ﴿for those on earth﴾ been explicit in generality, that division would not be valid.

The second: Suppose this text does convey generality, yet He, Exalted is He, related about the angels in the surah "Ha Mim, the Believer" that He said: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way"﴾ [Ghafir: 7].

The third: It is permissible that what is meant by seeking forgiveness is that He not hasten to punish them, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God holds back the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾ [Fatir: 41].

The fourth: It is permissible to say that they seek forgiveness for everyone on earth. As for the unbelievers, it is by way of requesting faith for them; as for the believers, it is by way of overlooking their misdeeds. For we say: "O God, guide the unbelievers, adorn their hearts with the light of faith, and remove from their thoughts the desolation of disbelief." This, in reality, is a seeking of forgiveness.

Know that His saying, ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those on earth﴾, indicates that they do not seek forgiveness for themselves. Had they been persisting in disobedience, their seeking forgiveness for themselves would have come before their seeking forgiveness for those on earth. Since God did not mention their seeking forgiveness for themselves, we know that they are free from all sins. The prophets, peace be upon them, do have sins, and one who has no sin whatsoever is superior to one who has sin. Also, His saying, ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those on earth﴾, indicates that they seek forgiveness for the prophets, because the prophets are among those on earth. And if they are seeking forgiveness for the prophets, peace be upon them, then the apparent conclusion is that they are superior to them.

When God, Exalted is He, related about the angels the glorification, the praise, and the seeking of forgiveness, He said: ﴿Unquestionably, God is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾. The purpose is to draw attention to the fact that although the angels seek forgiveness for humankind, absolute forgiveness and absolute mercy belong to the Truth, glorified and exalted is He. Its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: The angels' undertaking to request forgiveness for humankind from God, Exalted is He, happened only because God, Exalted is He, created in their hearts a motive to request that forgiveness. Had God, Exalted is He, not created in their hearts those motives, they would not have undertaken that request. Since this is so, the absolutely Forgiving and the absolutely Merciful is God, glorified and exalted is He.

The second: The angels said at the beginning of the matter: ﴿Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 30]. Then at the end of the matter they came to seek forgiveness for those on earth. As for the mercy and beneficence of the Truth, it was present in both the first and the last. Thus it is established that the absolutely Forgiving and the absolutely Merciful is God, Exalted is He.

The third: [p. 127] That He, Exalted is He, related about them that they seek forgiveness for those on earth, and He did not relate about them that they request mercy for those on earth. So He said: ﴿Unquestionably, God is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾, meaning that He gives the forgiveness they requested and adds to it complete and perfect mercy.

* * *

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And those who take protectors other than Him﴾, that is, who set up partners and equals to Him, ﴿God is Watchful over them﴾, that is, Observer of their conditions and their deeds, nothing of them escapes Him, and He will call them to account for them. There is no watcher over them except Him alone. And you, O Muhammad, are not entrusted with their affair, nor with compelling them to faith; you are only a warner.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 7–12 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it, and warn of the Day of Assembly, about which there is no doubt: a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze.﴾ ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whom He wills into His mercy. As for the wrongdoers, they have no protector or helper.﴾ ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him? But Allah is the Protector, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back.﴾ ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth. He made for you, from yourselves, mates, and among the cattle, mates. He multiplies you thereby. There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing.﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is Knowing of all things.﴾

Know that the word "ذلك" (dhalika, "that/thus") is used to point to something previously mentioned. So His saying, ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾, requires that the revelation of the Qur'an be compared to something already mentioned here. And there is nothing previously mentioned here to which the revelation of the Qur'an can be compared except His saying: ﴿And those who have taken protectors besides Him, Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾ [Ash-Shura: 6]. The meaning is: just as We revealed to you that you are not a watcher over them and not a guardian over them, so likewise We revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may be a warner to them.

As for His saying, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾, it means: that you may warn the people of the Mother of Cities, because a town does not understand, as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. The Mother of Cities (Umm al-Qura) is the origin of the towns, and it is Makkah. It was named by this name in honor of it, because the House (the Ka'bah) and the Station of Ibrahim are in it. The Arabs call the origin of everything its "mother," to the extent that it is said: "This poem is one of the mother-poems of so-and-so." And "those around it" are the people of the desert and the settled, and the people of the towns (ahl al-madar). And "warning" (al-indhar) is intimidation.

If it is said: the apparent wording requires that Allah revealed to him only to warn the people of Makkah and the towns surrounding Makkah, and this requires that he be a messenger only to them and not a messenger to all the worlds. The answer: the specification by mention does not indicate the negation of the ruling for what is other than it. So this verse indicates that he is a messenger to these specifically. And His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a comprehensive messenger to mankind﴾ [Saba': 28] indicates that he is a messenger to all the worlds. Also, once it was established that he was a messenger to the people of Makkah, it became obligatory that he be truthful. Then it has been transmitted to us by mass transmission (tawatur) that he used to claim that he was a messenger to all the worlds, and the truthful person, when he informs about something, it is obligatory to affirm him in it. Thus it is established that he is a messenger to all the worlds.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and warn of the Day of Assembly﴾. The original form is to say: "I warned so-and-so of such-and-such," so the required phrasing would have been: "that you may warn the Mother of Cities of the Day of Assembly." Also, there is an ellipsis here, and the implied meaning is: that you may warn the people of the Mother of Cities of the punishment of the Day of Assembly. Regarding naming it "the Day of Assembly," there are several aspects:

The first: that the creatures are gathered in it. He said: ﴿The Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly﴾ [At-Taghabun: 9]. So in it the people of the heavens gather with the people of the earth.

The second: that it gathers between the spirits and the bodies.

The third: that it gathers every doer with his deed.

The fourth: that it gathers the oppressor with the oppressed.

His saying ﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ is an attribute of the Day of Assembly, which is one about which there is no doubt. And His saying ﴿a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ means: on the Day of Assembly, whose attribute is that the people in it will be two parties, a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze. If it is said: His saying ﴿the Day of Assembly﴾ requires that the people be gathered together, and His saying ﴿a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ requires that they be separated, and combining the two attributes is impossible. We say: they are gathered first, and then they become two parties.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community﴾. The purpose is to establish His saying: ﴿And those who have taken protectors besides Him, Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾ [Ash-Shura: 6]. That is, it should not be within your power to compel them to faith. If Allah willed that, He would have done it, because He is more capable than you. But He made some believers and some disbelievers. So His saying ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ indicates that it is He, exalted is He, who admitted them into faith and obedience. And His saying ﴿As for the wrongdoers, they have no protector or helper﴾ means that He, exalted is He, did not admit them into His mercy. This indicates that the first group entered His mercy because they had a protector and a helper who admitted them into that mercy, whereas these had no protector or helper to admit them into His mercy.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ The meaning is: He, exalted is He, first related about them that they had taken protectors besides Him. Then He said after that to Muhammad (ﷺ): You are not a watcher over them or a guardian. And it is not obligatory upon you to compel them to faith, whether they wish or refuse. For if this matter were obligatory, Allah would have done it, because He is more capable than you. Then He repeated that statement after this, by way of rebuke, for His saying ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ is an interrogative in the form of denial.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But Allah is the Protector﴾. The fa' in His saying ﴿But Allah is the Protector﴾ is the answer to an implied conditional clause, as if He said: If they intend protectors in truth, then Allah is the Protector in truth; there is no protector other than Him, because He ''gives life to the dead and is over all things competent.'' So He is the one worthy of being taken as a protector, rather than one who has no power over anything.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: the connection of the verse is that, just as He prevented the Messenger (ﷺ) from compelling the disbelievers to faith by force, likewise He prevented the believers from entering into disputes and contentions with them. So He said: ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah﴾, which is the rewarding of those who are right in it and the punishing of the wrongdoers. It has also been said: "Whatever you differ about and dispute, then bring it for judgment to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the judgment of anyone else does not override his judgment." It has also been said: "Whatever disagreement has occurred among you concerning matters that do not pertain to your obligations, and for which you have no way to act, such as the reality of the soul, then say: Allah knows best about it." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you about the soul. Say: The soul is by the command of my Lord﴾ [Al-Isra': 85].

The second issue: the sense of the verse is as if He said: Say, O Muhammad: ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah﴾. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back.﴾

The third issue: those who deny analogy (nufat al-qiyas, the opponents of qiyas, analogical reasoning) argued with this verse. They said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah﴾ either means: its judgment is derived from the explicit text of Allah concerning it, or it means: its judgment is derived from analogy to what Allah has explicitly stated. The second is invalid, because it would require that all rulings be established by analogy, and that is invalid. So the first is adopted, and therefore all rulings must be established by explicit text, and that negates acting upon analogy. The opponent may say: Why could it not be that the meaning is: its judgment is known from the explanation of Allah, exalted is He, whether that explanation is by explicit text or by analogy? It is answered: the purpose of referring the matter to Allah is to end disagreement, and returning to analogy strengthens the disagreement rather than clarifying it. Therefore what is obligatory is returning to the explicit texts of Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is Allah, my Lord﴾, meaning: that judge between you is ﴿my Lord﴾. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ in repelling the plots of the enemies and in seeking every good. ﴿And to Him I turn back﴾, meaning: to Him I return in all important matters. And His saying ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ conveys restriction, meaning: I rely upon none but Him. This is an indication of the falsity of the way of those who take other than Allah as protector.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. It is read with the nominative (raf') and the genitive (jarr). The nominative is on the basis that it is the predicate of "that" (dhalikum), or the predicate of an omitted subject. The genitive is on the basis that the sentence is to be understood thus: "Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth." And His saying ﴿That is Allah, my Lord﴾ is a parenthetical clause that comes between the attribute and the thing described. ﴿He made for you, from yourselves﴾, that is, from your own kind, from among mankind, ﴿mates﴾, ﴿and among the cattle, mates﴾, meaning: He created mates from among the cattle. Its meaning is: and He also created for the cattle mates from among themselves. ﴿He multiplies you﴾, that is, He increases you in number. It is said: "Dhara'a Allah al-khalq," meaning, Allah multiplied the creation, that is, increased them in number. His saying ﴿thereby﴾ means: in this arrangement, which is marriage, namely that He made people and cattle into mates, so that between their males and females there is procreation and propagation. The pronoun in ﴿yadhra'ukum﴾ refers to those addressed, except that the side of humans was given precedence in it for two reasons:

The first: that the side of the rational was given precedence over the non-rational.

The second: that the side of those addressed was given precedence over the absent.

If it is asked: What is the meaning of ﴿yadhra'ukum﴾ in this arrangement, and why did He not say: ﴿yadhra'ukum bihi﴾ ("multiplies you by it")? We say: this arrangement is made like the source and the mine for this multiplication. Do you not see that it is said of living beings in the creation of mates that there is multiplication, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in retribution (qisas) there is life for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 179].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾. There are issues regarding this verse:

The first issue: the scholars of divine unity (ulama al-tawhid), in both earlier and later times, have used this verse as evidence for negating that He, exalted is He, is a composite body made of organs and parts, and existing in place and direction. They said: If He were a body, He would be a likeness to all other bodies, and so it would necessitate that likenesses and similarities belong to Him, and that is invalid by the explicit statement of His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. This argument can be presented in another way: it may be said: either the meaning of ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ is in the essential realities (ma'hiyyat al-dhat), or the meaning is that nothing is like unto Him in the attributes. The second is invalid, because servants are described as knowing and capable, just as Allah, exalted is He, is described with that; and likewise they are described as being known and mentioned, while Allah, exalted is He, is described with that. Thus it is established that the intended meaning of likeness is equality in the reality of the essence. So the meaning is that no essence equals Allah, exalted is He, in essential being. Therefore, if Allah, exalted is He, were a body, then His being a body would be His essence and not an attribute. Then, if all other bodies are equal to Him in bodyhood, meaning in being spatially bounded, long, wide, and deep, then all other bodies would be similar to the essence of Allah, exalted is He, in being an essence. And the text negates that. Therefore He must not be a body.

You should know that Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah cited our school's argument from this verse in the book he called *al-Tawhid* ("Divine Unity"), though in reality it is a book of *shirk* (polytheism). He then objected to it. I will mention the substance of his words after omitting the lengthy digressions, for he was a man of confused speech, of little understanding, and deficient intellect. He said:

"We affirm that God has a Face, and we say: the Face of our Lord possesses such light, radiance and splendour that, if its veil were lifted, the glories of His Face would burn up everything its sight reached. The Face of our Lord is free from perishing and annihilation. We say that the faces of the children of Adam have been decreed by God to perish and be annihilated, and He has denied them majesty and honour, and they are not described as having light, radiance or splendour. And if merely affirming a Face for God necessitated likening Him to creation, then whoever said that the children of Adam have faces, and that pigs, apes and dogs have faces, would have likened the faces of the children of Adam to the faces of pigs, apes and dogs."

He then said: "There is no doubt that this is the doctrine of the Jahmiyya (followers of Jahm ibn Safwan), for if it were said to him, 'Your face resembles the face of a pig or an ape,' he would become angry and would abuse the one who said it. Thus we know that affirming a Face and two Hands for God does not necessitate affirming likeness between God and His creation."

In another section of this book he mentioned: "The Qur'an indicates that equivalence occurs between the Essence of God, exalted is He, and His creation in many attributes, and this does not entail that the speaker is an anthropomorphist (mushabbih). So it is the same here." We shall enumerate the instances he mentioned, exhaustively.

The first: He, exalted is He, said in this verse, ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, and said concerning man, ﴿So We made him one who hears and sees﴾ [Al-Insan: 2].

The second: He said, ﴿And say: Work, and God will see your work, and so will His Messenger﴾ [At-Tawbah: 105], and said concerning created beings, ﴿Have they not seen the birds, subjected in the air of the sky?﴾ [An-Nahl: 79].

The third: He said, ﴿And construct the ark under Our eyes﴾ [Hud: 37], and ﴿So be patient for the judgement of your Lord, for indeed you are under Our eyes﴾ [At-Tur: 48], and said concerning created beings, ﴿You see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 83].

The fourth: He said to Iblis, ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My Two Hands?﴾ [Sad: 75], and said, ﴿Rather, His Two Hands are outstretched﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 64], and said concerning created beings, ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Al-Anfal: 51], ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Al-Hajj: 10], and ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God; the Hand of God is above their hands﴾ [Al-Fath: 10].

The fifth: He, exalted is He, said, ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], and said concerning those who ride animals, ﴿That you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 13], and said concerning the ark of Noah, ﴿And it came to rest upon al-Judi﴾ [Hud: 44].

The sixth: He named Himself ''the Mighty'' (al-'Aziz), saying, ﴿The Mighty, the Compeller﴾ [Al-Hashr: 23]. Then He applied this name to created beings in His words, ﴿O 'Aziz, indeed he has an aged father﴾ [Yusuf: 78], and ﴿O 'Aziz, adversity has touched us and our family﴾ [Yusuf: 88].

The seventh: He named Himself ''the King'' (al-Malik), and also named some of His servants ''king,'' saying, ﴿And the king said, bring him to me﴾ [Yusuf: 54]. He named Himself ''the Great'' (al-'Azim), then applied this name to a created being, saying, ﴿Lord of the Great Throne﴾ [At-Tawbah: 129]. He named Himself ''the Compeller, the Proud'' (al-Jabbar al-Mutakabbir), and applied this name to a created being, saying, ﴿Thus God seals every heart of a proud, compelling one﴾ [Ghafir: 35]."

He then elaborated at length on giving examples of this kind, and said: "Whoever considers the examples we have mentioned can multiply them." This is what this man put forward in this book.

[p. 131]

I say: this wretched ignorant man only fell into such fables because he did not know the reality of *al-mithlayn* (the two likes/equals). The scholars of *tawhid* have thoroughly investigated the discussion of the two likes, and then built upon it the argument from this verse. So we say: *al-mithlan* (the two like things) are those each of which occupies the place of the other in its reality and quiddity (mahiyya). The thorough treatment of this matter is preceded by another premise, so we say: what is considered in anything is either the complete quiddity of that thing, or a part of its quiddity, or a matter external to its quiddity but a necessary concomitant of that quiddity, or a matter external to its quiddity and not a necessary concomitant of it. This division is based on the distinction between the essence of a thing and the attributes subsisting in it, which is known by immediate perception. For we see a green unripe grape, extremely green and sour, later become extremely black and sweet. The essence remains, the attributes differ, and the remaining essence is other than the differing attributes. Likewise we see hair that was extremely black later become extremely white. The essence remains, the attributes change, and what remains is other than what changes. From what we have mentioned, it is clear that essences are other than attributes.

Having understood this, we say: the difference of attributes does not at all necessitate the difference of essences. For we see one body that was at rest, then becomes moving, then comes to rest again. The essences remain in all states in one manner and one order, while the attributes succeed one another and depart. Thus it is established that the difference of attributes and accidents does not necessitate the difference of essences.

Having understood this, we say: bodies out of which the face of a dog or ape is composed are equal to the bodies out of which the face of a human or a horse is composed. The difference arose only because of the subsisting accidents, namely colours, shapes, roughness, smoothness, and the presence or absence of sensation in it. So the difference arose only through the difference in attributes and accidents. As for the essences of bodies, they are alike. However, the common people do not know the difference between essences and attributes, so they say that the face of a human differs from the face of a donkey, and indeed they are right, for that difference came about through shape, colour and the other attributes. But bodies, insofar as they are bodies, are alike and equal. Thus it is established that the words this man put forward were mentioned only because he was one of the common people, and he did not know that what is considered in similarity and difference are the realities of things and their quiddities, not the accidents and attributes subsisting in them.

There remains the question: what is the proof that all bodies are alike? We say: we have here two standpoints.

The first standpoint: we say this premise is either granted or not granted. If it is granted, then the aim is achieved. If it is disputed, we say: why could it not be said that the God of the world is the sun, or the moon, or the sphere, or the Throne, or the Footstool, and that this body differs in quiddity from all other bodies, so that it is eternal, pre-eternal, necessarily existent, while all other bodies are originated and created? Even if the first and the last generations agreed to dispel this compulsion from the anthropomorphists, they would not be able to do so. If they say: this is false, because the Qur'an indicates that the sun, moon and all the spheres are originated and created, it is said: this is from the category of extreme foolishness, for the validity of the Qur'an and the validity of the prophethood of the prophets are founded upon knowledge of God. Therefore establishing the knowledge of God through the Qur'an and the word of the Prophet is something no rational person who understands what he is saying would say.

The second standpoint: the scholars of the principles of theology (usul) established a decisive proof that bodies are alike in essence and reality. When this is established, it becomes clear that if the God of the world were a body, His essence would be equal to the essences of bodies. But this is false by reason and by transmitted text. By reason: because if His essence were equal to the essences of all other bodies, then whatever is valid of all other bodies would have to be valid of Him, so it would necessitate that He is originated and created, susceptible to non-existence and annihilation, susceptible to dispersal and disintegration. As for transmitted text, it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾.

This completes the discussion of the presentation of this proof. At this point it becomes clear that we do not say that whenever equality in an attribute occurs, equality in the complete reality must follow. Rather we say: since it has been established that bodies are alike in complete quiddity, if His essence were a body, that body would be equal to all other bodies in complete quiddity. In that case, every body would necessarily be a like to Him, because we have shown that what is considered in the occurrence of likeness is consideration of realities as they are, not consideration of the attributes subsisting in them. It is thus made clear by the presentation we have given that the argument of the people of *tawhid* is extremely strong, and that these words which this man put forward were mentioned only because he was far from knowledge of realities, so he followed the manner of the words of the common people, and was deceived by those words he mentioned. We ask God, exalted is He, for a good end.

* * *

Second question: there is a difficulty in the apparent meaning of this verse. It is said: its intended purpose is the negation of a like from God, exalted is He, but its apparent meaning necessitates affirming a like for God. For it implies negating a like from His like, not from Him, and that necessitates affirming a like for God, exalted is He. The scholars answered this by saying that the Arabs say, "Someone like you does not stingy" (mithluka la yabkhalu), meaning "you do not stingy," so they negate stinginess from his like while intending to negate it from him. And a man says, "This speech is not said to someone like me," meaning "it is not said to me." The poet said:

"And one like me is like the trunks of palm trees."

The purpose of this is emphasis (mubalagha). For if that judgement is negated from one who resembles someone because of resembling him, then its negation from him himself is more fitting. Its parallel is their saying, "Peace upon the exalted assembly," and the intended meaning is: if God's peace falls upon His assembly and His place, then it is more fitting that it falls upon Him. Likewise here: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ means, "There is nothing like Him," as an emphasis in the manner we have mentioned. According to this interpretation, this expression is not superfluous and without effect, but gives emphasis in the manner we have mentioned.

Jahm ibn Safwan claimed that the intended purpose of this verse is to show that He, exalted is He, is not named by the name "thing" (shay'). He said: because everything would be a like to the like of itself, so His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ means "there is nothing like the like of Him," and this requires that He not be named by the name "thing." But in my view there is another route to this, which is that the intended purpose of combining the two particles of comparison is the proof that shows He is exalted above having a like. Its statement is that one says: if He had a like, He would be like His own self, and this is impossible; therefore affirming a like for Him is impossible. As for showing that if He had a like He would be like His own self, the matter there is evident. As for showing that this is impossible, it is because if He were like the like of His own self, He would be equal to His like in that quiddity and different from it in His own self, and what makes them share is other than what makes them differ. So the essence of each of the two would be composite, and every composite is contingent. Thus it is established that if a like were to occur for the Necessarily Existent, He would not be necessarily existent in Himself. Having understood this, His saying "there is nothing like the like of Him is a thing" indicates that if it were true of Him that He is a like of the like of His own self, He would not be a thing, based on what we have shown: that if a like occurred for the Necessarily Existent, He would not be necessarily existent. This is what the expression can bear.

Third question: this verse indicates the negation of a like, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾ [Ar-Rum: 27] requires affirming a likeness (mathal), so there must be a distinction between the two. We say: *mithl* (like) is that which is equal to a thing in complete quiddity, while *mathal* (likeness/example) is that which is equal to it in some attributes external to the quiddity, even if it differs in complete quiddity.

**Issue 4:** His saying ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, hears audible things and sees visible things. If it is said: it is impossible to apply this word to its apparent meaning, because when a striking or a tearing occurs, the air between those two bodies is violently displaced, so the air undulates because of that, and that undulation reaches the surface of the eardrum (al-ṣimākh). This is hearing. As for seeing, it is the pupil (al-ḥadaqa) being affected by the image of the seen object. Thus hearing and seeing are expressions for the affection of a sense organ (ḥāssa), and that is impossible for God. Therefore, applying hearing and seeing to His knowledge of audible and visible things is not permissible.

The answer: the proof that hearing is distinct from the affection of the sense organ is that when we hear a sound, we know from which direction it came. So we know that we perceived the sound where that sound exists in itself. This indicates that perceiving a sound is a state distinct from the impact on the eardrum caused by the undulation of that air.

As for seeing, the proof that it is a state distinct from the affection of the pupil is that the point of the eye is a small body, so it is impossible for a great image to be imprinted in it. We say: the imprinted image is small, while the seen image in the world itself is great. This indicates that seeing is distinct from that very imprinting. Given that this is established, we say: the impossibility of affection with respect to God does not necessitate the impossibility of hearing and seeing with respect to Him.

If they say: grant that hearing and seeing are two states distinct from the affection of the sense organ, yet their occurrence is conditioned upon the occurrence of that affection. Since that affection is impossible for God, the occurrence of hearing and seeing is impossible for God. We say: the apparent meaning of ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ indicates that He is hearing and seeing. So we may not depart from this apparent meaning unless there is proof that the faculty called hearing and seeing is conditioned upon the occurrence of affection, and affection is impossible for God, so that the occurrence of the faculty called hearing and seeing would be impossible. You, who claim this conditioning, are the ones who must provide proof of it. We hold fast to the apparent wording until you mention what requires departing from it.

If someone says: ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ implies restriction (ḥaṣr). What is the meaning of this restriction, given that the servants are also described as hearing and seeing? We say: al-Samī' (the All-Hearing) and al-Baṣīr (the All-Seeing) are words indicating the occurrence of these two attributes in the mode of perfection, and perfection in all attributes belongs only to God. This is what is meant by this restriction.

As for His saying ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾, know that the meaning of the verse is that He is the Originator (Fāṭir) of the heavens and the earth, and idols are not so. Also, He is the Creator of our selves and our spouses, and the Creator of our children from us and from our spouses, and idols are not so. Also, (﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾), and idols are not so. The purpose of all of this is to show the Capable, the Bestower, the Generous, the Merciful. How, then, is it permissible to make idols, which are inanimate objects, equal to Him in worship?

His saying ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾ means the keys (maqālīd, sing. miqlād) of provision from the heavens and the earth. The keys of the heavens are the rains, and the keys of the earth are the plants. We mentioned the explanation of maqālīd in Sūrat al-Zumar at His saying ﴿He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾, because the keys of sustenance are in His hand. ﴿Indeed, He is, of all things,﴾ regarding extending and measuring, ﴿Knowing﴾.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 7–12 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it, and warn of the Day of Assembly, about which there is no doubt: a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze.﴾ ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community, but He admits whom He wills into His mercy. As for the wrongdoers, they have no protector or helper.﴾ ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him? But Allah is the Protector, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things competent.﴾ ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah. That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back.﴾ ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth. He made for you, from yourselves, mates, and among the cattle, mates. He multiplies you thereby. There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing.﴾ ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth. He extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed, He is Knowing of all things.﴾

Know that the word "ذلك" (dhalika, "that/thus") is used to point to something previously mentioned. So His saying, ﴿And thus We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾, requires that the revelation of the Qur'an be compared to something already mentioned here. And there is nothing previously mentioned here to which the revelation of the Qur'an can be compared except His saying: ﴿And those who have taken protectors besides Him, Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾ [Ash-Shura: 6]. The meaning is: just as We revealed to you that you are not a watcher over them and not a guardian over them, so likewise We revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an, that you may be a warner to them.

As for His saying, ﴿that you may warn the Mother of Cities﴾, it means: that you may warn the people of the Mother of Cities, because a town does not understand, as in His saying: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. The Mother of Cities (Umm al-Qura) is the origin of the towns, and it is Makkah. It was named by this name in honor of it, because the House (the Ka'bah) and the Station of Ibrahim are in it. The Arabs call the origin of everything its "mother," to the extent that it is said: "This poem is one of the mother-poems of so-and-so." And "those around it" are the people of the desert and the settled, and the people of the towns (ahl al-madar). And "warning" (al-indhar) is intimidation.

If it is said: the apparent wording requires that Allah revealed to him only to warn the people of Makkah and the towns surrounding Makkah, and this requires that he be a messenger only to them and not a messenger to all the worlds. The answer: the specification by mention does not indicate the negation of the ruling for what is other than it. So this verse indicates that he is a messenger to these specifically. And His saying: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a comprehensive messenger to mankind﴾ [Saba': 28] indicates that he is a messenger to all the worlds. Also, once it was established that he was a messenger to the people of Makkah, it became obligatory that he be truthful. Then it has been transmitted to us by mass transmission (tawatur) that he used to claim that he was a messenger to all the worlds, and the truthful person, when he informs about something, it is obligatory to affirm him in it. Thus it is established that he is a messenger to all the worlds.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and warn of the Day of Assembly﴾. The original form is to say: "I warned so-and-so of such-and-such," so the required phrasing would have been: "that you may warn the Mother of Cities of the Day of Assembly." Also, there is an ellipsis here, and the implied meaning is: that you may warn the people of the Mother of Cities of the punishment of the Day of Assembly. Regarding naming it "the Day of Assembly," there are several aspects:

The first: that the creatures are gathered in it. He said: ﴿The Day He gathers you for the Day of Assembly﴾ [At-Taghabun: 9]. So in it the people of the heavens gather with the people of the earth.

The second: that it gathers between the spirits and the bodies.

The third: that it gathers every doer with his deed.

The fourth: that it gathers the oppressor with the oppressed.

His saying ﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ is an attribute of the Day of Assembly, which is one about which there is no doubt. And His saying ﴿a party will be in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ means: on the Day of Assembly, whose attribute is that the people in it will be two parties, a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze. If it is said: His saying ﴿the Day of Assembly﴾ requires that the people be gathered together, and His saying ﴿a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ requires that they be separated, and combining the two attributes is impossible. We say: they are gathered first, and then they become two parties.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have made them one community﴾. The purpose is to establish His saying: ﴿And those who have taken protectors besides Him, Allah is Watchful over them, and you are not a guardian over them﴾ [Ash-Shura: 6]. That is, it should not be within your power to compel them to faith. If Allah willed that, He would have done it, because He is more capable than you. But He made some believers and some disbelievers. So His saying ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ indicates that it is He, exalted is He, who admitted them into faith and obedience. And His saying ﴿As for the wrongdoers, they have no protector or helper﴾ means that He, exalted is He, did not admit them into His mercy. This indicates that the first group entered His mercy because they had a protector and a helper who admitted them into that mercy, whereas these had no protector or helper to admit them into His mercy.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ The meaning is: He, exalted is He, first related about them that they had taken protectors besides Him. Then He said after that to Muhammad (ﷺ): You are not a watcher over them or a guardian. And it is not obligatory upon you to compel them to faith, whether they wish or refuse. For if this matter were obligatory, Allah would have done it, because He is more capable than you. Then He repeated that statement after this, by way of rebuke, for His saying ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ is an interrogative in the form of denial.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But Allah is the Protector﴾. The fa' in His saying ﴿But Allah is the Protector﴾ is the answer to an implied conditional clause, as if He said: If they intend protectors in truth, then Allah is the Protector in truth; there is no protector other than Him, because He ''gives life to the dead and is over all things competent.'' So He is the one worthy of being taken as a protector, rather than one who has no power over anything.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah﴾. Regarding this there are several issues:

The first issue: the connection of the verse is that, just as He prevented the Messenger (ﷺ) from compelling the disbelievers to faith by force, likewise He prevented the believers from entering into disputes and contentions with them. So He said: ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah﴾, which is the rewarding of those who are right in it and the punishing of the wrongdoers. It has also been said: "Whatever you differ about and dispute, then bring it for judgment to the Messenger (ﷺ), and the judgment of anyone else does not override his judgment." It has also been said: "Whatever disagreement has occurred among you concerning matters that do not pertain to your obligations, and for which you have no way to act, such as the reality of the soul, then say: Allah knows best about it." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you about the soul. Say: The soul is by the command of my Lord﴾ [Al-Isra': 85].

The second issue: the sense of the verse is as if He said: Say, O Muhammad: ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah﴾. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back.﴾

The third issue: those who deny analogy (nufat al-qiyas, the opponents of qiyas, analogical reasoning) argued with this verse. They said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah﴾ either means: its judgment is derived from the explicit text of Allah concerning it, or it means: its judgment is derived from analogy to what Allah has explicitly stated. The second is invalid, because it would require that all rulings be established by analogy, and that is invalid. So the first is adopted, and therefore all rulings must be established by explicit text, and that negates acting upon analogy. The opponent may say: Why could it not be that the meaning is: its judgment is known from the explanation of Allah, exalted is He, whether that explanation is by explicit text or by analogy? It is answered: the purpose of referring the matter to Allah is to end disagreement, and returning to analogy strengthens the disagreement rather than clarifying it. Therefore what is obligatory is returning to the explicit texts of Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is Allah, my Lord﴾, meaning: that judge between you is ﴿my Lord﴾. ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ in repelling the plots of the enemies and in seeking every good. ﴿And to Him I turn back﴾, meaning: to Him I return in all important matters. And His saying ﴿Upon Him I have relied﴾ conveys restriction, meaning: I rely upon none but Him. This is an indication of the falsity of the way of those who take other than Allah as protector.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. It is read with the nominative (raf') and the genitive (jarr). The nominative is on the basis that it is the predicate of "that" (dhalikum), or the predicate of an omitted subject. The genitive is on the basis that the sentence is to be understood thus: "Whatever you differ about, its judgment belongs to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth." And His saying ﴿That is Allah, my Lord﴾ is a parenthetical clause that comes between the attribute and the thing described. ﴿He made for you, from yourselves﴾, that is, from your own kind, from among mankind, ﴿mates﴾, ﴿and among the cattle, mates﴾, meaning: He created mates from among the cattle. Its meaning is: and He also created for the cattle mates from among themselves. ﴿He multiplies you﴾, that is, He increases you in number. It is said: "Dhara'a Allah al-khalq," meaning, Allah multiplied the creation, that is, increased them in number. His saying ﴿thereby﴾ means: in this arrangement, which is marriage, namely that He made people and cattle into mates, so that between their males and females there is procreation and propagation. The pronoun in ﴿yadhra'ukum﴾ refers to those addressed, except that the side of humans was given precedence in it for two reasons:

The first: that the side of the rational was given precedence over the non-rational.

The second: that the side of those addressed was given precedence over the absent.

If it is asked: What is the meaning of ﴿yadhra'ukum﴾ in this arrangement, and why did He not say: ﴿yadhra'ukum bihi﴾ ("multiplies you by it")? We say: this arrangement is made like the source and the mine for this multiplication. Do you not see that it is said of living beings in the creation of mates that there is multiplication, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And in retribution (qisas) there is life for you﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 179].

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾. There are issues regarding this verse:

The first issue: the scholars of divine unity (ulama al-tawhid), in both earlier and later times, have used this verse as evidence for negating that He, exalted is He, is a composite body made of organs and parts, and existing in place and direction. They said: If He were a body, He would be a likeness to all other bodies, and so it would necessitate that likenesses and similarities belong to Him, and that is invalid by the explicit statement of His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. This argument can be presented in another way: it may be said: either the meaning of ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ is in the essential realities (ma'hiyyat al-dhat), or the meaning is that nothing is like unto Him in the attributes. The second is invalid, because servants are described as knowing and capable, just as Allah, exalted is He, is described with that; and likewise they are described as being known and mentioned, while Allah, exalted is He, is described with that. Thus it is established that the intended meaning of likeness is equality in the reality of the essence. So the meaning is that no essence equals Allah, exalted is He, in essential being. Therefore, if Allah, exalted is He, were a body, then His being a body would be His essence and not an attribute. Then, if all other bodies are equal to Him in bodyhood, meaning in being spatially bounded, long, wide, and deep, then all other bodies would be similar to the essence of Allah, exalted is He, in being an essence. And the text negates that. Therefore He must not be a body.

You should know that Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Khuzaymah cited our school's argument from this verse in the book he called *al-Tawhid* ("Divine Unity"), though in reality it is a book of *shirk* (polytheism). He then objected to it. I will mention the substance of his words after omitting the lengthy digressions, for he was a man of confused speech, of little understanding, and deficient intellect. He said:

"We affirm that God has a Face, and we say: the Face of our Lord possesses such light, radiance and splendour that, if its veil were lifted, the glories of His Face would burn up everything its sight reached. The Face of our Lord is free from perishing and annihilation. We say that the faces of the children of Adam have been decreed by God to perish and be annihilated, and He has denied them majesty and honour, and they are not described as having light, radiance or splendour. And if merely affirming a Face for God necessitated likening Him to creation, then whoever said that the children of Adam have faces, and that pigs, apes and dogs have faces, would have likened the faces of the children of Adam to the faces of pigs, apes and dogs."

He then said: "There is no doubt that this is the doctrine of the Jahmiyya (followers of Jahm ibn Safwan), for if it were said to him, 'Your face resembles the face of a pig or an ape,' he would become angry and would abuse the one who said it. Thus we know that affirming a Face and two Hands for God does not necessitate affirming likeness between God and His creation."

In another section of this book he mentioned: "The Qur'an indicates that equivalence occurs between the Essence of God, exalted is He, and His creation in many attributes, and this does not entail that the speaker is an anthropomorphist (mushabbih). So it is the same here." We shall enumerate the instances he mentioned, exhaustively.

The first: He, exalted is He, said in this verse, ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, and said concerning man, ﴿So We made him one who hears and sees﴾ [Al-Insan: 2].

The second: He said, ﴿And say: Work, and God will see your work, and so will His Messenger﴾ [At-Tawbah: 105], and said concerning created beings, ﴿Have they not seen the birds, subjected in the air of the sky?﴾ [An-Nahl: 79].

The third: He said, ﴿And construct the ark under Our eyes﴾ [Hud: 37], and ﴿So be patient for the judgement of your Lord, for indeed you are under Our eyes﴾ [At-Tur: 48], and said concerning created beings, ﴿You see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 83].

The fourth: He said to Iblis, ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My Two Hands?﴾ [Sad: 75], and said, ﴿Rather, His Two Hands are outstretched﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 64], and said concerning created beings, ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Al-Anfal: 51], ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [Al-Hajj: 10], and ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to God; the Hand of God is above their hands﴾ [Al-Fath: 10].

The fifth: He, exalted is He, said, ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], and said concerning those who ride animals, ﴿That you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 13], and said concerning the ark of Noah, ﴿And it came to rest upon al-Judi﴾ [Hud: 44].

The sixth: He named Himself ''the Mighty'' (al-'Aziz), saying, ﴿The Mighty, the Compeller﴾ [Al-Hashr: 23]. Then He applied this name to created beings in His words, ﴿O 'Aziz, indeed he has an aged father﴾ [Yusuf: 78], and ﴿O 'Aziz, adversity has touched us and our family﴾ [Yusuf: 88].

The seventh: He named Himself ''the King'' (al-Malik), and also named some of His servants ''king,'' saying, ﴿And the king said, bring him to me﴾ [Yusuf: 54]. He named Himself ''the Great'' (al-'Azim), then applied this name to a created being, saying, ﴿Lord of the Great Throne﴾ [At-Tawbah: 129]. He named Himself ''the Compeller, the Proud'' (al-Jabbar al-Mutakabbir), and applied this name to a created being, saying, ﴿Thus God seals every heart of a proud, compelling one﴾ [Ghafir: 35]."

He then elaborated at length on giving examples of this kind, and said: "Whoever considers the examples we have mentioned can multiply them." This is what this man put forward in this book.

[p. 131]

I say: this wretched ignorant man only fell into such fables because he did not know the reality of *al-mithlayn* (the two likes/equals). The scholars of *tawhid* have thoroughly investigated the discussion of the two likes, and then built upon it the argument from this verse. So we say: *al-mithlan* (the two like things) are those each of which occupies the place of the other in its reality and quiddity (mahiyya). The thorough treatment of this matter is preceded by another premise, so we say: what is considered in anything is either the complete quiddity of that thing, or a part of its quiddity, or a matter external to its quiddity but a necessary concomitant of that quiddity, or a matter external to its quiddity and not a necessary concomitant of it. This division is based on the distinction between the essence of a thing and the attributes subsisting in it, which is known by immediate perception. For we see a green unripe grape, extremely green and sour, later become extremely black and sweet. The essence remains, the attributes differ, and the remaining essence is other than the differing attributes. Likewise we see hair that was extremely black later become extremely white. The essence remains, the attributes change, and what remains is other than what changes. From what we have mentioned, it is clear that essences are other than attributes.

Having understood this, we say: the difference of attributes does not at all necessitate the difference of essences. For we see one body that was at rest, then becomes moving, then comes to rest again. The essences remain in all states in one manner and one order, while the attributes succeed one another and depart. Thus it is established that the difference of attributes and accidents does not necessitate the difference of essences.

Having understood this, we say: bodies out of which the face of a dog or ape is composed are equal to the bodies out of which the face of a human or a horse is composed. The difference arose only because of the subsisting accidents, namely colours, shapes, roughness, smoothness, and the presence or absence of sensation in it. So the difference arose only through the difference in attributes and accidents. As for the essences of bodies, they are alike. However, the common people do not know the difference between essences and attributes, so they say that the face of a human differs from the face of a donkey, and indeed they are right, for that difference came about through shape, colour and the other attributes. But bodies, insofar as they are bodies, are alike and equal. Thus it is established that the words this man put forward were mentioned only because he was one of the common people, and he did not know that what is considered in similarity and difference are the realities of things and their quiddities, not the accidents and attributes subsisting in them.

There remains the question: what is the proof that all bodies are alike? We say: we have here two standpoints.

The first standpoint: we say this premise is either granted or not granted. If it is granted, then the aim is achieved. If it is disputed, we say: why could it not be said that the God of the world is the sun, or the moon, or the sphere, or the Throne, or the Footstool, and that this body differs in quiddity from all other bodies, so that it is eternal, pre-eternal, necessarily existent, while all other bodies are originated and created? Even if the first and the last generations agreed to dispel this compulsion from the anthropomorphists, they would not be able to do so. If they say: this is false, because the Qur'an indicates that the sun, moon and all the spheres are originated and created, it is said: this is from the category of extreme foolishness, for the validity of the Qur'an and the validity of the prophethood of the prophets are founded upon knowledge of God. Therefore establishing the knowledge of God through the Qur'an and the word of the Prophet is something no rational person who understands what he is saying would say.

The second standpoint: the scholars of the principles of theology (usul) established a decisive proof that bodies are alike in essence and reality. When this is established, it becomes clear that if the God of the world were a body, His essence would be equal to the essences of bodies. But this is false by reason and by transmitted text. By reason: because if His essence were equal to the essences of all other bodies, then whatever is valid of all other bodies would have to be valid of Him, so it would necessitate that He is originated and created, susceptible to non-existence and annihilation, susceptible to dispersal and disintegration. As for transmitted text, it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾.

This completes the discussion of the presentation of this proof. At this point it becomes clear that we do not say that whenever equality in an attribute occurs, equality in the complete reality must follow. Rather we say: since it has been established that bodies are alike in complete quiddity, if His essence were a body, that body would be equal to all other bodies in complete quiddity. In that case, every body would necessarily be a like to Him, because we have shown that what is considered in the occurrence of likeness is consideration of realities as they are, not consideration of the attributes subsisting in them. It is thus made clear by the presentation we have given that the argument of the people of *tawhid* is extremely strong, and that these words which this man put forward were mentioned only because he was far from knowledge of realities, so he followed the manner of the words of the common people, and was deceived by those words he mentioned. We ask God, exalted is He, for a good end.

* * *

Second question: there is a difficulty in the apparent meaning of this verse. It is said: its intended purpose is the negation of a like from God, exalted is He, but its apparent meaning necessitates affirming a like for God. For it implies negating a like from His like, not from Him, and that necessitates affirming a like for God, exalted is He. The scholars answered this by saying that the Arabs say, "Someone like you does not stingy" (mithluka la yabkhalu), meaning "you do not stingy," so they negate stinginess from his like while intending to negate it from him. And a man says, "This speech is not said to someone like me," meaning "it is not said to me." The poet said:

"And one like me is like the trunks of palm trees."

The purpose of this is emphasis (mubalagha). For if that judgement is negated from one who resembles someone because of resembling him, then its negation from him himself is more fitting. Its parallel is their saying, "Peace upon the exalted assembly," and the intended meaning is: if God's peace falls upon His assembly and His place, then it is more fitting that it falls upon Him. Likewise here: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ means, "There is nothing like Him," as an emphasis in the manner we have mentioned. According to this interpretation, this expression is not superfluous and without effect, but gives emphasis in the manner we have mentioned.
