And His saying ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ is interpreted to mean that the best course, when you commit that earning, is the sending down of these afflictions upon you. The same applies to the answer regarding the remaining proofs. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** The adherents of metempsychosis (al-tanasukh) used this verse, as did those who say that children and animals do not feel pain. They said: the verse indicates that afflictions occur only due to a prior offense. Then the adherents of metempsychosis said: but these afflictions befall children and animals, so it must be that they committed sins in a previous time. As for those who say that children and animals have no pain, they said: it is established that these children and animals did not exist in another body, because of the corruption of the view of metempsychosis; therefore it is necessary to be certain that they do not feel pain, since pain is an affliction. The reply: His saying, the Exalted,

[Page 149]

﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is for what your hands have earned﴾ is addressed to one who understands and reasons, so animals and children are not included in it. The Exalted did not say that all that befalls animals of hardships is due to a prior sin. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ requires attributing the earning (kasb) to the hand. He said: earning does not occur through the hand, but through the power that resides in the hand. If the intended meaning of the word "hand" here is power, and this figurative usage is well known and in common use, then the word "hand" mentioned with regard to Allah the Exalted must be interpreted as power, to exalt Allah the Exalted above organs and parts. And Allah knows best.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He pardons much﴾. Its meaning is that He, exalted is He, may leave aside much of these afflictions out of His grace and mercy. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "We visited Imran ibn Husayn during a severe ailment, and it was said to him: 'We are truly saddened for you because of some of what we see.' He said: 'Do not do that. By God, what is dearest to Him is dearest to me.' Then he recited: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾, and said: 'This is for what my hands have earned, and my Lord's pardon will come to me.'" Abu Sakhla also related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: "Whatever Allah has pardoned, He is too mighty and too generous to return to it in the Hereafter, and whatever He has punished for in this world, Allah is too generous to repeat the punishment for it in the Hereafter." Al-Wahidi related it in al-Basit, and said: "If this is so, then this is the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, because Allah, exalted is He, has made the sins of the believers of two kinds: one kind He expiates for them through calamities in this world, and another kind He pardons them for in this world, and He is Generous and does not retract His pardon. This is the way of Allah with the believers. As for the disbeliever, He does not hasten the punishment for his sin until he meets his Lord on the Day of Resurrection."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He pardons much﴾. Its meaning is that He, exalted is He, may leave aside much of these afflictions out of His grace and mercy. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "We visited Imran ibn Husayn during a severe ailment, and it was said to him: 'We are truly saddened for you because of some of what we see.' He said: 'Do not do that. By God, what is dearest to Him is dearest to me.' Then he recited: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾, and said: 'This is for what my hands have earned, and my Lord's pardon will come to me.'" Abu Sakhla also related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: "Whatever Allah has pardoned, He is too mighty and too generous to return to it in the Hereafter, and whatever He has punished for in this world, Allah is too generous to repeat the punishment for it in the Hereafter." Al-Wahidi related it in al-Basit, and said: "If this is so, then this is the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, because Allah, exalted is He, has made the sins of the believers of two kinds: one kind He expiates for them through calamities in this world, and another kind He pardons them for in this world, and He is Generous and does not retract His pardon. This is the way of Allah with the believers. As for the disbeliever, He does not hasten the punishment for his sin until he meets his Lord on the Day of Resurrection."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you cannot escape in the earth﴾. He says: you, O assembly of polytheists, cannot escape in the earth; that is, you cannot overpower Me wherever you are, so you cannot outrun Me by means of your fleeing in the earth. ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾. The intended ones are those who worship idols; He made clear that there is absolutely no benefit in them. The helper is Allah, exalted is He; therefore He alone is the one whose worship is fitting.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 27–31 (part 1 of 2):**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth; but He sends down in measure what He wills. Indeed, He is Acquainted with and Seeing of His servants.﴾ ﴿And it is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired, and spreads His mercy. And He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed in them of living creatures. And He is over their gathering, when He wills, All-Capable.﴾ ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is for what your hands have earned, and He pardons much.﴾ ﴿And you cannot escape within the earth, and you have no protector or helper other than Allah.﴾

There are several issues in this verse:

**The first issue:** Know that when He, the Exalted, said in the previous verse that He answers the supplication of the believers, a question arose: the believer may be in hardship, affliction and poverty, then he supplicates and sees no effect of the answer. What then is the situation regarding this, given what preceded it in His saying ﴿and He responds to those who believe﴾? Allah the Exalted answered it with His saying ﴿And if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth﴾, meaning: they would have proceeded to acts of disobedience. Since that is to be feared, it is necessary that He not give them what they asked for. Al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) said: this verse proves the falsity of the view of the Mujbira (the Determinists) in two respects:

The first: the sense of the statement is that He, the Exalted, ﴿if Allah were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth﴾, and rebellion in the earth is not willed. So the will to expand provision is not realized. This statement is complete only if we say that He wills rebellion in the earth, and that necessitates the corruption of the view of the Mujbira.

The second: He, the Exalted, clarified that He did not will to expand provision only because it would lead to harm. Since He, the Exalted, has clarified that He does not will what leads to harm, then it is more fitting that He not be willing harm itself. Our companions (the Ash'aris) replied: the strong inclination toward rebellion, cruelty and domination is an attribute that came into being after it was not. It must therefore have an agent, and the agent of these states is either the servant or Allah. The first is invalid, because he only does these things if his nature inclines toward them. The question then returns: who originated that second inclination? And an infinite regress (tasalsul) follows. Also, a strong inclination toward injustice and cruelty is a defect and deficiency, and the intelligent person does not accept bringing upon himself the causes of deficiency. Since this has been refuted, it is established that the originator of this inclination and desire is Allah the Exalted. Then al-Jubba'i, in his tafsir, raised an objection against himself. He said: If it is said, has He not expanded provision for some of His servants while they rebelled? He answered it by saying that the one who had provision and rebelled, it was known of his condition that he would rebel in every case, whether he was given that provision or not. I say: this answer is false, and the Qur'an and reason refute it.

[Page 147]

As for the Qur'an, it is His saying ﴿Indeed, man does transgress, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-Alaq: 6–7]. He issued a general judgment that the attainment of wealth is a cause of the attainment of transgression. As for reason, when the soul inclines toward evil but lacks the instruments and tools, the evil is less; when it possesses them, the evil is greater. Thus it is established that finding wealth necessitates transgression.

**The second issue:** In explaining the aspect for which expansion necessitates transgression, they mentioned several aspects:

The first: if Allah the Exalted were to equalize provision among all, it would be impossible for some to serve others, and if the matter became so, the world would be ruined and the interests would be disrupted.

The second: this verse is specific to the Arabs. Whenever their provision expanded, and they found rain that quenched their thirst and pasture and herbage that satisfied them, they proceeded to plunder and raid.

The third: man is naturally proud. When he finds wealth and power, he returns to the requirement of his original nature, which is arrogance. When he falls into hardship, affliction and what is disliked, he is broken, and returns to obedience and humility.

**The third issue:** Khabbab ibn al-Aratt said: this verse was revealed concerning us, for we looked at the wealth of Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir and Banu Qaynuqa', and we desired it. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the People of the Suffa, who wished for abundance of provision and wealth.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yunzilu﴾ (يُنْزِلُ) with a light (unshaddated) pronunciation, and the rest with the shadda (intensified form, يُنَزِّلُ). Then we say: ﴿bi-qadarin﴾ (بِقَدَرٍ) means "by measure" (بِتَقْدِيرٍ). It is said: qadara-hu qadran and qadaran. ﴿Indeed, He is Acquainted with and Seeing of His servants﴾ means that He knows the conditions of people, their natures, and the consequences of their affairs, so He apportions their provisions according to their interests. When He, the Exalted, clarified that He does not give them more than the measure of their need, because He knew that that surplus would harm their religion, He clarified that if they are in need of provision, He does not withhold it from them. So He said: ﴿And it is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired﴾. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read ﴿yunazzilu﴾ with the shadda, and the rest without it. The author of al-Kashshaf said: ﴿qanatu﴾ (قَنَطُوا) has been read with a fatha and with a kasra on the nun. Sending down rain after despair is more conducive to gratitude, because the joy at obtaining a blessing after affliction is more complete, so its recipient is more inclined to give thanks. ﴿And spreads His mercy﴾, meaning the blessings of the rain, its benefits, and the fertility that results from it. It is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was said to him: "Drought has intensified and people have despaired." He said: "Then they will be rained upon," intending this verse. It is also permissible that he intends His vast mercy in everything, as if it were said: He sends down the mercy which is the rain, and spreads all other kinds of mercy. ﴿And He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy﴾: "al-Waliyy" is the one who takes charge of His servants with His kindness, and "al-Hamid" is the one praised for what He conveys to creation of the kinds of mercy. Then He mentioned another sign that indicates His divinity, saying: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and what He has dispersed in them of living creatures﴾. We say: as for the indication of the creation of the heavens and the earth for the existence of the Wise God, we have already mentioned it. Likewise, the indication of the existence of animals for the existence of the Wise God. If it is said: how is it permissible to apply the word "dabba" (living creature) to the angels? We say: there are several aspects:

The first: an action is sometimes attributed to a group, even if its doer is one of them. It is said: "the sons of so-and-so did such-and-such," when only one of them did it. From this is His saying: ﴿From both of them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾ [al-Rahman: 22].

The second: ad-daba (الدَّبِيبُ) is movement, and the angels have movement.

The third: it is not unlikely that it is said that He, the Exalted, created in the heavens kinds of living creatures that walk on the earth in the manner of humans.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And He is over their gathering, when He wills, All-Capable﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "idha" (إذا) enters upon the present tense just as it enters upon the past tense. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ [al-Layl: 1], and from it is ﴿when He wills, All-Capable﴾. The intent is that He, the Exalted, created them scattered, not from incapacity, but for an interest; therefore He said: ﴿And He is over their gathering, when He wills, All-Capable﴾, meaning the gathering for the Resurrection

[Page 148]

and the reckoning. He said ﴿over their gathering﴾ and not ﴿over their gathering﴾ (in the feminine), because the purpose of this gathering is the reckoning, so it is as if He, the Exalted, said: He is over the gathering of the rational beings, when He wills, All-Capable. Al-Jubba'i argued from His saying ﴿when He wills, All-Capable﴾ that His will is originated, saying: the word "idha" indicates a temporal adverb, and the word "yasha'" (He wills) is the form of the future. If His will were eternal, there would be no benefit in specifying it with that determined time in the future. Since His saying ﴿when He wills, All-Capable﴾ indicates this specification, we know that His will is originated.

The reply: just as these two words entered upon the will, i.e., the will of Allah, they also entered upon the word "Qadir" (All-Capable). It would follow from this that His being capable would be an originated attribute. Since this is false, the same applies to what he mentioned. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is for what your hands have earned﴾. In the verse there are issues:

**The first issue:** Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿bi-ma kasabat﴾ (بِما كَسَبَتْ) without the fa' (فاء), and likewise it is so in the mushafs of Syria and Medina; the rest read it with the fa', and likewise it is so in their mushafs. The reading of the first has the analysis that "ma" (ما) is a subject in the sense of "that which," and "bi-ma kasabat" is its predicate, and the meaning is: "that which struck you occurred because of what your hands have earned." The analysis of the second is that the word "ma" is taken to carry the sense of a conditional.

**The second issue:** The intended meaning of these afflictions is the disagreeable states, such as pains, sicknesses, drought, drowning, thunderbolts and the like. They differed concerning pains such as these, whether they are punishments for past sins or not. Some of them denied that for several reasons:

The first: His saying ﴿On the Day every soul will be recompensed for what it earned﴾ [Ghafir: 17]. The Exalted clarified that recompense occurs only on the Day of Resurrection. He, the Exalted, said in the surah al-Fatiha ﴿Master of the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Fatiha: 4], meaning the Day of Recompense, and they agreed that what is intended by it is the Day of Resurrection.

The second: the afflictions of this world are shared by the heretic (zindiq) and the truthful (siddiq). What is like this cannot be considered punishment for sins. Rather, induction indicates that the occurrence of these afflictions to the righteous and the pious is more frequent than to the sinners. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "Affliction is most severe upon the prophets, then the saints, then the best of people, then the next best."

The third: this world is the abode of obligation (taklif). If recompense were made in it, the world would be both the abode of obligation and the abode of recompense together, and that is impossible.

As for those who say that these afflictions may be recompense for previous sins, they have held fast to what was narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "No harm befalls the son of Adam, not even the scratch of a twig, except for a sin," or words of this meaning. They also held fast to this verse, and to His saying ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things﴾ [al-Nisa: 160], and also to His saying after this verse ﴿Or He destroys them for what they have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 34], which is an explicit statement that that destruction was due to their earning.

The earlier scholars replied to their use of this verse, saying: the occurrence of these afflictions is by way of trial within obligation, not by way of punishment, as is the case with the prophets and saints. And His saying ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ is interpreted to mean that the best course, when you commit that earning, is the sending down of these afflictions upon you. The same applies to the answer regarding the remaining proofs. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** The adherents of metempsychosis (al-tanasukh) used this verse, as did those who say that children and animals do not feel pain. They said: the verse indicates that afflictions occur only due to a prior offense. Then the adherents of metempsychosis said: but these afflictions befall children and animals, so it must be that they committed sins in a previous time. As for those who say that children and animals have no pain, they said: it is established that these children and animals did not exist in another body, because of the corruption of the view of metempsychosis; therefore it is necessary to be certain that they do not feel pain, since pain is an affliction. The reply: His saying, the Exalted,

[Page 149]

﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is for what your hands have earned﴾ is addressed to one who understands and reasons, so animals and children are not included in it. The Exalted did not say that all that befalls animals of hardships is due to a prior sin. And Allah knows best.

**The fourth issue:** His saying ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ requires attributing the earning (kasb) to the hand. He said: earning does not occur through the hand, but through the power that resides in the hand. If the intended meaning of the word "hand" here is power, and this figurative usage is well known and in common use, then the word "hand" mentioned with regard to Allah the Exalted must be interpreted as power, to exalt Allah the Exalted above organs and parts. And Allah knows best.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He pardons much﴾. Its meaning is that He, exalted is He, may leave aside much of these afflictions out of His grace and mercy. It is related from al-Hasan that he said: "We visited Imran ibn Husayn during a severe ailment, and it was said to him: 'We are truly saddened for you because of some of what we see.' He said: 'Do not do that. By God, what is dearest to Him is dearest to me.' Then he recited: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾, and said: 'This is for what my hands have earned, and my Lord's pardon will come to me.'" Abu Sakhla also related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: "Whatever Allah has pardoned, He is too mighty and too generous to return to it in the Hereafter, and whatever He has punished for in this world, Allah is too generous to repeat the punishment for it in the Hereafter." Al-Wahidi related it in al-Basit, and said: "If this is so, then this is the most hopeful verse in the Book of Allah, because Allah, exalted is He, has made the sins of the believers of two kinds: one kind He expiates for them through calamities in this world, and another kind He pardons them for in this world, and He is Generous and does not retract His pardon. This is the way of Allah with the believers. As for the disbeliever, He does not hasten the punishment for his sin until he meets his Lord on the Day of Resurrection."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you cannot escape in the earth﴾. He says: you, O assembly of polytheists, cannot escape in the earth; that is, you cannot overpower Me wherever you are, so you cannot outrun Me by means of your fleeing in the earth. ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾. The intended ones are those who worship idols; He made clear that there is absolutely no benefit in them. The helper is Allah, exalted is He; therefore He alone is the one whose worship is fitting.

[p. 150]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among His signs are the ships running upon the sea like mountains﴾. ﴿If He wills, He calms the wind, and they remain motionless on its surface. Indeed in that are signs for everyone who is patient and grateful﴾. ﴿Or He wrecks them for what they have earned, and pardons much﴾.

[p. 151]
﴿And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no escape﴾. ﴿Whatever you have been given is only the enjoyment of the worldly life. But what is with God is better and more lasting for those who believe and put their trust in their Lord﴾. ﴿And those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, and when they are angry, they forgive﴾. ﴿And those who respond to their Lord, establish the prayer, whose affair is decided by consultation among themselves, and who spend from what We have provided them﴾. ﴿And those who, when injustice afflicts them, defend themselves﴾.

There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "al-jawari" with a yā' both in continuation (waṣl) and in pause (waqf). Retaining the yā' is the original form, and omitting it is for lightness.

The second issue: "al-jawari" means "the ships that run", and the noun being described (the ships) is omitted because there is no ambiguity.

The third issue: Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned among His signs these great ships that run over the surface of the sea when the winds blow. Know that the purpose of mentioning them is two things:

The first: that they be taken as evidence for the existence of the All-Powerful, All-Wise.

The second: that the great blessings God has bestowed on His servants in them be made known.

As for the first aspect: they agree that "al-a'lam" refers to the mountains. Al-Khansa said in her elegy for her brother:

"Indeed Sakhr is one whom the guided take as their guide, as if he were a banner with fire upon its head."

It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked her to recite this poem, and when the narrator reached this line, he said: "May God fight her! She was not content to liken him to a mountain until she put fire on its top!" Having understood this, we say: these great ships, which are like mountains, run over the surface of the sea when the winds blow at the swiftest speeds, and when these winds become still, they stop. We have already shown with proof in Surat al-Nahl that the mover and stiller of the winds is God, exalted is He, since no human can move them or still them. This indicates the existence of the All-Powerful God. Also, a ship is extremely heavy, yet despite its weight it remains upon the surface of the water, which is another proof.

As for the second aspect, knowing the benefits in them: He, exalted is He, assigned to each side of the earth a different kind of goods, and when the goods of one side are transported to the other side by ships, and vice versa, great benefits arise in trade. For these reasons God, exalted is He, mentioned the condition of these ships.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If He wills, He calms the wind, and they remain motionless on its surface﴾. Abu 'Amr and the majority read "in yashha'" with a hamza, because the sukun on the hamza is the sign of the jussive (jazm). Warsh, from Nafi', reads it without a hamza. Nafi' alone reads "yuskin al-riyah" in the plural, and the rest read "al-rih" in the singular. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "yazlalna" is read with fatḥa and kasra on the lām, from "zalla yazallu" and "yazillu". His saying, exalted is He, ﴿rawakid﴾ means "fixed" (rawatib), that is, they do not run over its surface, meaning over the surface of the sea. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for everyone who is patient﴾ under God's trial, ﴿grateful﴾ for His blessings. The purpose is to alert that the believer must never be heedless of the evidences of knowing God, because he is necessarily either in trial or in blessings. If he is in trial, he is among the patient, and if he is in blessings, he is among the grateful. In either case, he is never among the heedless.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Or He wrecks them for what they have earned﴾, meaning: or He destroys them. It is said "awbaqahu", meaning "he destroyed him", and it is said of a criminal, "his sins wrecked him", meaning "destroyed him". The meaning is that, if He wills, He tests those travelling on the sea with one of two afflictions: either He stills the wind, so the ships become motionless and stop on the back of the sea, or He sends violent winds against them so that they perish by drowning. In this case, His saying ﴿or He wrecks them﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿He calms﴾, because the meaning is: if He wills, He calms the wind so they remain still, or He stirs it up so they drown by its storm. His saying ﴿and pardons much﴾ means: if He wills, He destroys some people and saves others by way of pardoning them. If it is asked: what is the meaning of including pardon under the ruling of wrecking, since it is made jussive like it? We say: the meaning is: if He wills, He destroys some people and saves others by way of pardoning them. As for the one who reads "wa-ya'fu", he has begun a new sentence (isti'naf).

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And those who dispute concerning Our signs will know that they have no escape﴾. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "yā'lamu" with ḍammah, as a new sentence (isti'naf). The rest read it with fatḥa. The reading with ḍammah is a new sentence. As for the fatḥa, it is conjoined to an omitted cause (ta'lil maḥdhuf), whose estimate is: "so that He may take vengeance upon them", and "and that those who dispute concerning Our signs may know". Conjoining to an omitted cause is not rare in the Qur'an, and among its examples is His saying: ﴿and so that We may make it a sign for people﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God created the heavens and the earth in truth, and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 22]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: whoever reads "wa-ya'lam" with jazm, it is as if He said: "or if He wills", combining three matters: the destruction of one people, the salvation of another people, and the warning of others.

Having understood this, we say: the meaning of the verse, ﴿and those who dispute﴾, that is, who contend by way of denial, will know that there is no escape for them when the ships stand still and when the winds blow violently. That will be the cause of their acknowledging that the God who benefits and harms is none but God.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the evidences of divine oneness (tawhid), He followed them with a warning about the world and a belittling of its status. This is because what prevents acceptance of evidence is only the desire for the world, due to leadership and the pursuit of status. When the world becomes small in a man's eyes, he does not turn to it, and then he benefits from the mention of the evidences. So He said: ﴿Whatever you have been given is only the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾. He called it "enjoyment" to alert to its scarcity and worthlessness, and because sense perception testifies that everything connected with the world is quick to vanish and end.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But what is with God is better and more lasting﴾. The meaning is that the aims of the world are base and perishing, and He alerted to their baseness by calling them "enjoyment", and alerted to their passing by making them of "the worldly". As for the Hereafter, it is "better and more lasting". Clear reason requires preferring the lasting good over the base and perishing. Then He explained that this superiority is achieved only by one who is described by certain attributes:

The first attribute: that he be among the believers, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿for those who believe﴾.

The second attribute: that he be among those who rely upon the grace of God, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿and put their trust in their Lord﴾. As for one who supposes that obedience necessitates reward, he relies upon his own deed and not upon God, so he does not fall under the verse.

The third attribute: that they avoid the major sins and immoralities. Ibn 'Abbas said: "the major sin" is polytheism (shirk), as transmitted by the author of al-Kashshaf. But in my view this is far-fetched, because the condition of belief was mentioned first, and that suffices against polytheism. It was also said: the intended meaning of "major sins" is what relates to innovations (bida') and the drawing out of doubts, and "immoralities" is what relates to the appetitive faculty (al-quwwa al-shahwaniyya). His saying ﴿and when they are angry, they forgive﴾ relates to the irascible faculty (al-quwwa al-ghadabiyya). He specifically tied anger to the word "forgiveness" because anger is of the nature of fire, its dominance is strong, and resisting it is difficult. For this reason He specified it with this word. And God knows best.

The fourth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who respond to their Lord﴾. What is meant is complete submission. If they say: since He made belief a condition for it, does not the response to God enter into belief? We say: in my view it is closer to interpret this as contentment with God's decree from the depth of the heart, and that there is no dispute in the heart concerning any matter.

When He mentioned this condition, He said: ﴿and establish the prayer﴾. What is meant is the establishment of the obligatory prayers, because this is the condition for obtaining reward.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿whose affair is decided by consultation among themselves﴾. It was said: whenever an incident occurred among them, they gathered and consulted. So God praised them, meaning: they do not act on one opinion alone, but do not proceed in anything on which they have not agreed. It is related from al-Hasan: "No people consult together but they are guided to the most rightful course of their affair." Consultation (shura) is a verbal noun like futya, in the sense of mutual consulting. The meaning of His saying ﴿whose affair is decided by consultation among themselves﴾ is: "possessing consultation".

The fifth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when injustice afflicts them, defend themselves﴾. The meaning is that they limit their self-defence to what God has allowed them and do not go beyond it. It is related from al-Nakha'i that when he recited it he said: "They used to dislike humiliating themselves, so that foolish people would not dare against them."

If it is asked: this verse is problematic for two reasons:

The first: since before it He mentioned ﴿and when they are angry, they forgive﴾, how does it fit that there be mentioned alongside it what runs as its opposite, namely His saying ﴿and those who, when injustice afflicts them, defend themselves﴾?

The second: all verses indicate that pardon is better. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that you pardon is closer to piety﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. He said: ﴿and when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]. He said: ﴿Take what is easy, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]. He said: ﴿And if you punish, punish with the like of what you were punished with. But if you are patient, it is better for the patient﴾ [al-Nahl: 126]. These verses contradict the implication of this verse. The answer: pardon is of two kinds:

One: that pardon be a cause of calming strife, the offender's wrongdoing, and his return from his wrongdoing.

The second: that pardon become a cause of greater boldness in the offender and of greater strength in his rage and anger.

Then He made clear that pardon is more excellent, by His saying: ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is upon God﴾. Thus the question is resolved, and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 40–48 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And whoever avenges himself after being wronged, those—there is no blame upon them.﴾ ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right. Those will have a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ ﴿And you will see them exposed to it, humbled from disgrace, looking with sidelong glances. And those who believed will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers will be in lasting punishment."﴾ ﴿And they will have no protectors to support them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And those who, when tyranny strikes them, they defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 39], He followed it with what indicates that this self-defence must be restricted to an equal measure, for deficiency is injustice, excess is oppression, and equality is justice, by which the heavens and the earth stand. For this reason He said, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: One may say, "The retaliation for an evil is legislated and permitted, so how is it called an evil?" The author of al-Kashshaf answered this: both acts are called by the same name; the first deed, and its recompense, is an evil because it harms the one upon whom it falls. He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [al-Nisa: 78], meaning what displeases them of calamities and afflictions. Others answered that when one of the two was placed opposite the other, by way of metaphor, the name of one was applied to the other. The truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

The second issue: This verse is a great foundation in the science of jurisprudence (fiqh, the science of legal rulings derived from the sources). Its implication is that every offence should be met with its like. This is because leaving aggression unchecked opens the door to evil and transgression, since injustice, oppression and aggression are in the nature of every person. If he is not restrained from it, he will proceed with it and not abandon it. As for exceeding the measure of the offence, that is injustice, and the Sharia is free of it. Thus there remains only that it be met with an equal. Then this text was reinforced by other texts, such as His saying, ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿Prescribed for you is retribution for the murdered﴾ [al-Baqara: 178]. Retribution (qisas, the principle of equal retaliation) is an expression of equality and parity. His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45], and His saying, ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾ [al-Baqara: 179]. All these texts together require the requiting of a thing with its like.

Then here is a subtle point: when the right cannot be secured except by taking more than the equal, a conflict arises between inflicting additional harm on the offender and preventing the wronged party from securing his right. Which takes precedence? This is the place of the effort of the jurists (ijtihad), and this differs according to the different cases. Some matters have been derived from this principle, as a reminder of the rest.

The first example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that a Muslim is not killed for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection), and a free person is not killed for a slave, saying: Equivalence is a condition for the application of retribution, and it is absent in these two cases, so retribution must not apply between them. As for proving that equivalence is a condition for retribution, it is the texts mentioned, and the way to argue from them is this: either we take the equivalence mentioned in these texts as equivalence in all matters except what the evidence has specified, or we take it as equivalence in one specific matter. The second is weaker, because that specific matter is not mentioned in the verse, so if we read the verse as referring to it, it would entail ambiguity; and if we read the text as referring to the first sense, it would entail specification (takhsis, restricting a general text). It is known that removing ambiguity takes precedence over removing specification. So it is established that the verse requires observing equivalence in all matters, except what is specified by rational proof and by a separate textual proof. Given this, we say: observing equivalence in the killing of a Muslim for a dhimmi, and in the killing of a free person for a slave, is not possible, because Islam is regarded by the Sharia in imposing execution, either to establish it when it is absent, as in the case of an original disbeliever, or to preserve it when it is present, as in the case of an apostate. Also, freedom is a quality that the Sharia regards for judgeship, leadership, and testimony. Thus it is established that equivalence is a condition for the application of retribution, and it is absent here, so retribution must be prevented.

The second example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that hands are cut off for a single hand. He said: There is no doubt that when all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of those who cut, or from some of them, then it is required that the same be legislated against those cutters, by these texts. Whoever says that cutting is legislated, either in whole or in part, against all of them or some of them, has said that it is obligatory upon all. It remains to be said that this would entail taking more than the equal from the offender, which is forbidden. However, we say: when a conflict arose between the side of the offender and the side of the wronged party, the side of the wronged party takes precedence in consideration.

The third example: The partner of a father (in killing his child) is subject to retribution, and the proof of this is that the wounding proceeded from him, so he must be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾. When this is established, the full retribution is established too, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The fourth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever burns (someone), we burn him, and whoever drowns (someone), we drown him. The proof for this is these texts indicating the requiting of each thing with its like.

The fifth example: The witnesses in a retribution case, if they recant and say, "We deliberately lied," they are liable to retribution, because by that testimony they caused the blood of the accused to be wasted. Therefore their blood must become wasted, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The sixth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The one who is coerced is liable to retribution, because killing proceeded from him unjustly, so it is required that a like be imposed upon him. As for killing proceeding from him, the senses indicate it. As for its being unjust, that is because the Muslims unanimously agreed that he is charged by Allah, the Exalted, not to kill, and they unanimously agreed that by it he deserves a great sin and severe punishment. Given this, it is required that he be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The seventh example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Killing with a blunt object requires retribution. The proof for this is that the offender nullified his life, so the guardian of the one killed must be enabled to nullify the life of the killer, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The eighth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution. Although we mentioned this issue in the first example, we mention here another way of explanation. We say: the killer destroyed for the owner of the slave something worth, for instance, ten dinars. Therefore he is obliged to pay ten dinars, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And when compensation becomes obligatory, retribution must not become obligatory, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The ninth example: The usufruct of usurped property is liable to compensation according to Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The proof for this is that the usurper caused the owner to lose benefits that by custom are valued at one dinar. Therefore he must cause the usurper to lose a like amount of property, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And whoever requires that this amount be lost by the usurper also says that it must be paid to the one from whom it was usurped.

The tenth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution, because if he were killed for a slave, he would be equal to the slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and by the rest of the texts we have recited. Furthermore, his own slave is killed in retribution for his own slave. Therefore the slave of another must be equal to his own slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by these very texts we have cited. On this assumption, his own slave is equal to the slave of another in the meanings that necessitate retribution, so his own slave is a like of the like of himself, and the like of a like is a like. Therefore it is required that his own slave be a like of himself in the meanings that necessitate retribution. If a free person were killed for the slave of another, he would be killing himself by the explanation we have given, and he is not killed for his own slave. Therefore he must not be killed for the slave of another.

We have mentioned these ten examples as derivations from this verse. Whoever is guided by discernment will find it easy to derive many of the matters of the Sharia from this principle. And Allah knows best.

Here there is a discussion. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the cutting of hands: There is no doubt that all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of them or some of them. However, it is not possible to secure that right except by taking more than the equal, because the loss of ten hands is greater than the loss of one hand. Therefore it must remain under the original prohibition. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If the loss of ten hands in return for one hand were forbidden, then the loss of ten lives in return for one life would be forbidden, because the loss of a life includes the loss of a hand. So if the loss of ten hands in return for one hand is forbidden, then the loss of ten lives for one life includes what is forbidden. Whatever includes what is forbidden is itself forbidden. Thus the killing of ten lives in return for one life ought to be forbidden. Since we are agreed that it is not forbidden, we know that what you mentioned about taking more than the equal is not prohibited by the Sharia. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: We have made clear that His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, requires the observance of equivalence absolutely, in all circumstances, except in what the evidence has specified. The jurists have introduced specification into it in many cases, sometimes based on another text inferior to it, and sometimes based on analogy (qiyas). There is no doubt that whoever claims specification bears the burden of proof. The responsible person is sufficient to hold to this text in all claims. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: If he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," then he may say to him, "May Allah disgrace you." But if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then he does not have that right; rather, the prescribed punishment is what Allah has commanded.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, between himself and his adversary, through pardon and overlooking, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. ﴿His reward is with Allah﴾: this is a general promise whose matter is not measured in greatness.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: The purpose of it is to draw attention to the fact that the wronged party is not permitted to take more than the equal from the wrongdoer, because the wrongdoer, beyond his own wrongdoing, is protected. Self-defence is hardly secure from exceeding the equal and from transgression, especially in the state of war and the flaring up of zeal. Thus the wronged person may, at the time of proceeding to take retribution, become a wrongdoer. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: Whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand up." He said:
[p. 156]
Then a group will stand up, and it will be said to them: "What is your reward with Allah?" They will say: "We are the ones who pardoned those who wronged us." It will be said to them: "Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah, the Exalted."

**Second point:** When Allah, exalted is He, urged forgiveness of the wrongdoer, He informed that, despite this, He does not love him. This is a reminder that if He does not love such a person, yet it is still recommended to pardon him, then the believer, who is the beloved of Allah by virtue of his faith, is more deserving of pardoning him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, meaning after the wrongdoer's injustice toward him. This is an instance of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. ﴿Those—there is no blame upon them﴾, meaning the ones who defend themselves, ﴿no blame upon them﴾ such as punishment or censure, because they have acted in accordance with what was permitted to them of retaliation (intisar).

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse to demonstrate that the consequential harm (sirayah) of retaliatory punishment (qawad) is not liable. He said: The Law either says that He permitted him to cut [the offender] absolutely, or on the condition that no consequential harm results from it. The second is invalid, because the original ruling concerning cutting is prohibition. So if the permission to cut is conditioned on the absence of consequential harm, and this condition is unknown, that cutting must remain under the original ruling of prohibition, because the original ruling concerning it is prohibition, and permissibility is achieved only when it is conditioned on an unknown condition. Therefore it must remain under the original ruling of prohibition. Since this is not the case, we know that the Law permitted him to cut in whatever manner it occurs, whether harm results or not. If that is so, then that consequential harm must not be liable, because he has defended himself after being wronged. Therefore no one may have any blame upon him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾, meaning those who begin the injustice, ﴿and transgress in the earth without right. For them is a painful punishment.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ The meaning: ﴿And whoever is patient﴾ by not seeking retribution, ﴿and forgives﴾ and overlooks, ﴿indeed, that﴾ patience and overlooking ﴿is of the matters requiring determination﴾, meaning that his resolve to abandon retaliation is among the commendable matters requiring determination. The returning pronoun has been omitted because it is understood, just as it is omitted in the saying "ghee is two manns for a dirham." It is narrated that a man reviled another man in the gathering of al-Hasan, and the one being reviled kept silent, perspiring, and wiping off his sweat. Then he stood up and recited this verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it, and comprehended it, when the ignorant had neglected it."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him.﴾ That is, there is no helper for him who can take charge of him after his abandonment, meaning after Allah has led him astray. This is explicit in permitting that Allah, exalted is He, leads astray, and that guidance is not within the power of anyone other than Allah, exalted is He. The Qadi said: The intended meaning is: whoever Allah leads astray from Paradise, for him there is no protector after Him to help him. The response: restricting misguidance to this specific form is contrary to the evidence. Moreover, Allah did not lead him astray from Paradise according to your view; rather, he led himself astray from Paradise.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ The meaning is that they seek to return to the world because of the enormity of the punishment they witness. Then He mentioned their condition when the Fire is presented to them, saying: ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled from abasement﴾, meaning while they are humbled, debased, and disgraced because of the humiliation that has befallen them. Then He said: ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾, meaning their gaze begins with a faint, hidden movement of the eyelids, stealthily, like one who is certain to be killed looking at the sword: he looks at it as though he cannot open his eyelids upon it and fill his eyes with it, as he does when looking at beloved things.

If it is said: Did He not say, describing the disbelievers, that they will be gathered blind? How then does He say here that they look with a furtive glance? We say: Perhaps they are like this at the beginning and then are made blind; or perhaps this applies to one group, and that to another.

When Allah described the condition of the disbelievers, He related what the believers say about them, saying: ﴿And those who believe will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "On the Day of Resurrection" may either be connected to "lost", or the statement of the believers may be occurring in this world; or it may be connected to "said", meaning: they will say on the Day of Resurrection when they see them in that condition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment.﴾ That is, enduring. The Qadi said: This indicates that the disbeliever and the sinner will have their punishment endure. The response: the unqualified term "wrongdoer" in the Qur'an is specific to the disbeliever. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers.﴾ What confirms this is that He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿And they will have no protectors to help them besides Allah.﴾ The meaning is that the idols they worshipped in the hope that they would intercede for them with Allah, exalted is He, did not bring that intercession. It is known that this applies only to the disbelievers. Then He said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ This indicates that the one who misguides and the one who guides is Allah, exalted is He, according to what is our statement and our school of thought. And Allah knows best.

[p. 157]

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. However, we say: when a conflict arose between the side of the offender and the side of the wronged party, the side of the wronged party takes precedence in consideration.

The third example: The partner of a father (in killing his child) is subject to retribution, and the proof of this is that the wounding proceeded from him, so he must be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾. When this is established, the full retribution is established too, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

Given this, it is required that he be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

Therefore he is obliged to pay ten dinars, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. Therefore the slave of another must be equal to his own slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by these very texts we have cited. On this assumption, his own slave is equal to the slave of another in the meanings that necessitate retribution, so his own slave is a like of the like of himself, and the like of a like is a like. Therefore it is required that his own slave be a like of himself in the meanings that necessitate retribution. If a free person were killed for the slave of another, he would be killing himself by the explanation we have given, and he is not killed for his own slave. Therefore he must not be killed for the slave of another.

We have mentioned these ten examples as derivations from this verse. Whoever is guided by discernment will find it easy to derive many of the matters of the Sharia from this principle. And Allah knows best.

Here there is a discussion. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the cutting of hands: There is no doubt that all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of them or some of them. Therefore it must remain under the original prohibition.
