Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, meaning after the wrongdoer's injustice toward him. This is an instance of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. ﴿Those—there is no blame upon them﴾, meaning the ones who defend themselves, ﴿no blame upon them﴾ such as punishment or censure, because they have acted in accordance with what was permitted to them of retaliation (intisar).

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse to demonstrate that the consequential harm (sirayah) of retaliatory punishment (qawad) is not liable. He said: The Law either says that He permitted him to cut [the offender] absolutely, or on the condition that no consequential harm results from it. The second is invalid, because the original ruling concerning cutting is prohibition. So if the permission to cut is conditioned on the absence of consequential harm, and this condition is unknown, that cutting must remain under the original ruling of prohibition, because the original ruling concerning it is prohibition, and permissibility is achieved only when it is conditioned on an unknown condition. Therefore it must remain under the original ruling of prohibition. Since this is not the case, we know that the Law permitted him to cut in whatever manner it occurs, whether harm results or not. If that is so, then that consequential harm must not be liable, because he has defended himself after being wronged. Therefore no one may have any blame upon him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾, meaning those who begin the injustice, ﴿and transgress in the earth without right. For them is a painful punishment.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ The meaning: ﴿And whoever is patient﴾ by not seeking retribution, ﴿and forgives﴾ and overlooks, ﴿indeed, that﴾ patience and overlooking ﴿is of the matters requiring determination﴾, meaning that his resolve to abandon retaliation is among the commendable matters requiring determination. The returning pronoun has been omitted because it is understood, just as it is omitted in the saying "ghee is two manns for a dirham." It is narrated that a man reviled another man in the gathering of al-Hasan, and the one being reviled kept silent, perspiring, and wiping off his sweat. Then he stood up and recited this verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it, and comprehended it, when the ignorant had neglected it."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him.﴾ That is, there is no helper for him who can take charge of him after his abandonment, meaning after Allah has led him astray. This is explicit in permitting that Allah, exalted is He, leads astray, and that guidance is not within the power of anyone other than Allah, exalted is He. The Qadi said: The intended meaning is: whoever Allah leads astray from Paradise, for him there is no protector after Him to help him. The response: restricting misguidance to this specific form is contrary to the evidence. Moreover, Allah did not lead him astray from Paradise according to your view; rather, he led himself astray from Paradise.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ The meaning is that they seek to return to the world because of the enormity of the punishment they witness. Then He mentioned their condition when the Fire is presented to them, saying: ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled from abasement﴾, meaning while they are humbled, debased, and disgraced because of the humiliation that has befallen them. Then He said: ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾, meaning their gaze begins with a faint, hidden movement of the eyelids, stealthily, like one who is certain to be killed looking at the sword: he looks at it as though he cannot open his eyelids upon it and fill his eyes with it, as he does when looking at beloved things.

If it is said: Did He not say, describing the disbelievers, that they will be gathered blind? How then does He say here that they look with a furtive glance? We say: Perhaps they are like this at the beginning and then are made blind; or perhaps this applies to one group, and that to another.

When Allah described the condition of the disbelievers, He related what the believers say about them, saying: ﴿And those who believe will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "On the Day of Resurrection" may either be connected to "lost", or the statement of the believers may be occurring in this world; or it may be connected to "said", meaning: they will say on the Day of Resurrection when they see them in that condition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment.﴾ That is, enduring. The Qadi said: This indicates that the disbeliever and the sinner will have their punishment endure. The response: the unqualified term "wrongdoer" in the Qur'an is specific to the disbeliever. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers.﴾ What confirms this is that He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿And they will have no protectors to help them besides Allah.﴾ The meaning is that the idols they worshipped in the hope that they would intercede for them with Allah, exalted is He, did not bring that intercession. It is known that this applies only to the disbelievers. Then He said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ This indicates that the one who misguides and the one who guides is Allah, exalted is He, according to what is our statement and our school of thought. And Allah knows best.

[p. 157]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 40–48 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And whoever avenges himself after being wronged, those—there is no blame upon them.﴾ ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right. Those will have a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ ﴿And you will see them exposed to it, humbled from disgrace, looking with sidelong glances. And those who believed will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers will be in lasting punishment."﴾ ﴿And they will have no protectors to support them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And those who, when tyranny strikes them, they defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 39], He followed it with what indicates that this self-defence must be restricted to an equal measure, for deficiency is injustice, excess is oppression, and equality is justice, by which the heavens and the earth stand. For this reason He said, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: One may say, "The retaliation for an evil is legislated and permitted, so how is it called an evil?" The author of al-Kashshaf answered this: both acts are called by the same name; the first deed, and its recompense, is an evil because it harms the one upon whom it falls. He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [al-Nisa: 78], meaning what displeases them of calamities and afflictions. Others answered that when one of the two was placed opposite the other, by way of metaphor, the name of one was applied to the other. The truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

The second issue: This verse is a great foundation in the science of jurisprudence (fiqh, the science of legal rulings derived from the sources). Its implication is that every offence should be met with its like. This is because leaving aggression unchecked opens the door to evil and transgression, since injustice, oppression and aggression are in the nature of every person. If he is not restrained from it, he will proceed with it and not abandon it. As for exceeding the measure of the offence, that is injustice, and the Sharia is free of it. Thus there remains only that it be met with an equal. Then this text was reinforced by other texts, such as His saying, ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿Prescribed for you is retribution for the murdered﴾ [al-Baqara: 178]. Retribution (qisas, the principle of equal retaliation) is an expression of equality and parity. His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45], and His saying, ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾ [al-Baqara: 179]. All these texts together require the requiting of a thing with its like.

Then here is a subtle point: when the right cannot be secured except by taking more than the equal, a conflict arises between inflicting additional harm on the offender and preventing the wronged party from securing his right. Which takes precedence? This is the place of the effort of the jurists (ijtihad), and this differs according to the different cases. Some matters have been derived from this principle, as a reminder of the rest.

The first example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that a Muslim is not killed for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection), and a free person is not killed for a slave, saying: Equivalence is a condition for the application of retribution, and it is absent in these two cases, so retribution must not apply between them. As for proving that equivalence is a condition for retribution, it is the texts mentioned, and the way to argue from them is this: either we take the equivalence mentioned in these texts as equivalence in all matters except what the evidence has specified, or we take it as equivalence in one specific matter. The second is weaker, because that specific matter is not mentioned in the verse, so if we read the verse as referring to it, it would entail ambiguity; and if we read the text as referring to the first sense, it would entail specification (takhsis, restricting a general text). It is known that removing ambiguity takes precedence over removing specification. So it is established that the verse requires observing equivalence in all matters, except what is specified by rational proof and by a separate textual proof. Given this, we say: observing equivalence in the killing of a Muslim for a dhimmi, and in the killing of a free person for a slave, is not possible, because Islam is regarded by the Sharia in imposing execution, either to establish it when it is absent, as in the case of an original disbeliever, or to preserve it when it is present, as in the case of an apostate. Also, freedom is a quality that the Sharia regards for judgeship, leadership, and testimony. Thus it is established that equivalence is a condition for the application of retribution, and it is absent here, so retribution must be prevented.

The second example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that hands are cut off for a single hand. He said: There is no doubt that when all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of those who cut, or from some of them, then it is required that the same be legislated against those cutters, by these texts. Whoever says that cutting is legislated, either in whole or in part, against all of them or some of them, has said that it is obligatory upon all. It remains to be said that this would entail taking more than the equal from the offender, which is forbidden. However, we say: when a conflict arose between the side of the offender and the side of the wronged party, the side of the wronged party takes precedence in consideration.

The third example: The partner of a father (in killing his child) is subject to retribution, and the proof of this is that the wounding proceeded from him, so he must be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾. When this is established, the full retribution is established too, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The fourth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever burns (someone), we burn him, and whoever drowns (someone), we drown him. The proof for this is these texts indicating the requiting of each thing with its like.

The fifth example: The witnesses in a retribution case, if they recant and say, "We deliberately lied," they are liable to retribution, because by that testimony they caused the blood of the accused to be wasted. Therefore their blood must become wasted, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The sixth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The one who is coerced is liable to retribution, because killing proceeded from him unjustly, so it is required that a like be imposed upon him. As for killing proceeding from him, the senses indicate it. As for its being unjust, that is because the Muslims unanimously agreed that he is charged by Allah, the Exalted, not to kill, and they unanimously agreed that by it he deserves a great sin and severe punishment. Given this, it is required that he be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The seventh example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Killing with a blunt object requires retribution. The proof for this is that the offender nullified his life, so the guardian of the one killed must be enabled to nullify the life of the killer, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The eighth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution. Although we mentioned this issue in the first example, we mention here another way of explanation. We say: the killer destroyed for the owner of the slave something worth, for instance, ten dinars. Therefore he is obliged to pay ten dinars, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And when compensation becomes obligatory, retribution must not become obligatory, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The ninth example: The usufruct of usurped property is liable to compensation according to Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The proof for this is that the usurper caused the owner to lose benefits that by custom are valued at one dinar. Therefore he must cause the usurper to lose a like amount of property, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And whoever requires that this amount be lost by the usurper also says that it must be paid to the one from whom it was usurped.

The tenth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution, because if he were killed for a slave, he would be equal to the slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and by the rest of the texts we have recited. Furthermore, his own slave is killed in retribution for his own slave. Therefore the slave of another must be equal to his own slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by these very texts we have cited. On this assumption, his own slave is equal to the slave of another in the meanings that necessitate retribution, so his own slave is a like of the like of himself, and the like of a like is a like. Therefore it is required that his own slave be a like of himself in the meanings that necessitate retribution. If a free person were killed for the slave of another, he would be killing himself by the explanation we have given, and he is not killed for his own slave. Therefore he must not be killed for the slave of another.

We have mentioned these ten examples as derivations from this verse. Whoever is guided by discernment will find it easy to derive many of the matters of the Sharia from this principle. And Allah knows best.

Here there is a discussion. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the cutting of hands: There is no doubt that all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of them or some of them. However, it is not possible to secure that right except by taking more than the equal, because the loss of ten hands is greater than the loss of one hand. Therefore it must remain under the original prohibition. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If the loss of ten hands in return for one hand were forbidden, then the loss of ten lives in return for one life would be forbidden, because the loss of a life includes the loss of a hand. So if the loss of ten hands in return for one hand is forbidden, then the loss of ten lives for one life includes what is forbidden. Whatever includes what is forbidden is itself forbidden. Thus the killing of ten lives in return for one life ought to be forbidden. Since we are agreed that it is not forbidden, we know that what you mentioned about taking more than the equal is not prohibited by the Sharia. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: We have made clear that His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, requires the observance of equivalence absolutely, in all circumstances, except in what the evidence has specified. The jurists have introduced specification into it in many cases, sometimes based on another text inferior to it, and sometimes based on analogy (qiyas). There is no doubt that whoever claims specification bears the burden of proof. The responsible person is sufficient to hold to this text in all claims. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: If he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," then he may say to him, "May Allah disgrace you." But if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then he does not have that right; rather, the prescribed punishment is what Allah has commanded.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, between himself and his adversary, through pardon and overlooking, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. ﴿His reward is with Allah﴾: this is a general promise whose matter is not measured in greatness.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: The purpose of it is to draw attention to the fact that the wronged party is not permitted to take more than the equal from the wrongdoer, because the wrongdoer, beyond his own wrongdoing, is protected. Self-defence is hardly secure from exceeding the equal and from transgression, especially in the state of war and the flaring up of zeal. Thus the wronged person may, at the time of proceeding to take retribution, become a wrongdoer. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: Whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand up." He said:
[p. 156]
Then a group will stand up, and it will be said to them: "What is your reward with Allah?" They will say: "We are the ones who pardoned those who wronged us." It will be said to them: "Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah, the Exalted."

**Second point:** When Allah, exalted is He, urged forgiveness of the wrongdoer, He informed that, despite this, He does not love him. This is a reminder that if He does not love such a person, yet it is still recommended to pardon him, then the believer, who is the beloved of Allah by virtue of his faith, is more deserving of pardoning him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, meaning after the wrongdoer's injustice toward him. This is an instance of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. ﴿Those—there is no blame upon them﴾, meaning the ones who defend themselves, ﴿no blame upon them﴾ such as punishment or censure, because they have acted in accordance with what was permitted to them of retaliation (intisar).

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse to demonstrate that the consequential harm (sirayah) of retaliatory punishment (qawad) is not liable. He said: The Law either says that He permitted him to cut [the offender] absolutely, or on the condition that no consequential harm results from it. The second is invalid, because the original ruling concerning cutting is prohibition. So if the permission to cut is conditioned on the absence of consequential harm, and this condition is unknown, that cutting must remain under the original ruling of prohibition, because the original ruling concerning it is prohibition, and permissibility is achieved only when it is conditioned on an unknown condition. Therefore it must remain under the original ruling of prohibition. Since this is not the case, we know that the Law permitted him to cut in whatever manner it occurs, whether harm results or not. If that is so, then that consequential harm must not be liable, because he has defended himself after being wronged. Therefore no one may have any blame upon him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾, meaning those who begin the injustice, ﴿and transgress in the earth without right. For them is a painful punishment.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ The meaning: ﴿And whoever is patient﴾ by not seeking retribution, ﴿and forgives﴾ and overlooks, ﴿indeed, that﴾ patience and overlooking ﴿is of the matters requiring determination﴾, meaning that his resolve to abandon retaliation is among the commendable matters requiring determination. The returning pronoun has been omitted because it is understood, just as it is omitted in the saying "ghee is two manns for a dirham." It is narrated that a man reviled another man in the gathering of al-Hasan, and the one being reviled kept silent, perspiring, and wiping off his sweat. Then he stood up and recited this verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it, and comprehended it, when the ignorant had neglected it."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him.﴾ That is, there is no helper for him who can take charge of him after his abandonment, meaning after Allah has led him astray. This is explicit in permitting that Allah, exalted is He, leads astray, and that guidance is not within the power of anyone other than Allah, exalted is He. The Qadi said: The intended meaning is: whoever Allah leads astray from Paradise, for him there is no protector after Him to help him. The response: restricting misguidance to this specific form is contrary to the evidence. Moreover, Allah did not lead him astray from Paradise according to your view; rather, he led himself astray from Paradise.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ The meaning is that they seek to return to the world because of the enormity of the punishment they witness. Then He mentioned their condition when the Fire is presented to them, saying: ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled from abasement﴾, meaning while they are humbled, debased, and disgraced because of the humiliation that has befallen them. Then He said: ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾, meaning their gaze begins with a faint, hidden movement of the eyelids, stealthily, like one who is certain to be killed looking at the sword: he looks at it as though he cannot open his eyelids upon it and fill his eyes with it, as he does when looking at beloved things.

If it is said: Did He not say, describing the disbelievers, that they will be gathered blind? How then does He say here that they look with a furtive glance? We say: Perhaps they are like this at the beginning and then are made blind; or perhaps this applies to one group, and that to another.

When Allah described the condition of the disbelievers, He related what the believers say about them, saying: ﴿And those who believe will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "On the Day of Resurrection" may either be connected to "lost", or the statement of the believers may be occurring in this world; or it may be connected to "said", meaning: they will say on the Day of Resurrection when they see them in that condition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment.﴾ That is, enduring. The Qadi said: This indicates that the disbeliever and the sinner will have their punishment endure. The response: the unqualified term "wrongdoer" in the Qur'an is specific to the disbeliever. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers.﴾ What confirms this is that He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿And they will have no protectors to help them besides Allah.﴾ The meaning is that the idols they worshipped in the hope that they would intercede for them with Allah, exalted is He, did not bring that intercession. It is known that this applies only to the disbelievers. Then He said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ This indicates that the one who misguides and the one who guides is Allah, exalted is He, according to what is our statement and our school of thought. And Allah knows best.

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And whoever avenges himself after being wronged, those—there is no blame upon them.﴾ ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right. Those will have a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him. Whoever says that cutting is legislated, either in whole or in part, against all of them or some of them, has said that it is obligatory upon all. It remains to be said that this would entail taking more than the equal from the offender, which is forbidden. However, we say: when a conflict arose between the side of the offender and the side of the wronged party, the side of the wronged party takes precedence in consideration.

The third example: The partner of a father (in killing his child) is subject to retribution, and the proof of this is that the wounding proceeded from him, so he must be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾. When this is established, the full retribution is established too, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The fourth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever burns (someone), we burn him, and whoever drowns (someone), we drown him. The proof for this is these texts indicating the requiting of each thing with its like.

The fifth example: The witnesses in a retribution case, if they recant and say, "We deliberately lied," they are liable to retribution, because by that testimony they caused the blood of the accused to be wasted. Therefore their blood must become wasted, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The sixth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The one who is coerced is liable to retribution, because killing proceeded from him unjustly, so it is required that a like be imposed upon him. As for killing proceeding from him, the senses indicate it. As for its being unjust, that is because the Muslims unanimously agreed that he is charged by Allah, the Exalted, not to kill, and they unanimously agreed that by it he deserves a great sin and severe punishment. Given this, it is required that he be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The seventh example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Killing with a blunt object requires retribution. The proof for this is that the offender nullified his life, so the guardian of the one killed must be enabled to nullify the life of the killer, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The eighth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution. Although we mentioned this issue in the first example, we mention here another way of explanation. We say: the killer destroyed for the owner of the slave something worth, for instance, ten dinars. Therefore he is obliged to pay ten dinars, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And when compensation becomes obligatory, retribution must not become obligatory, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The ninth example: The usufruct of usurped property is liable to compensation according to Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The proof for this is that the usurper caused the owner to lose benefits that by custom are valued at one dinar. Therefore he must cause the usurper to lose a like amount of property, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And whoever requires that this amount be lost by the usurper also says that it must be paid to the one from whom it was usurped.

The tenth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution, because if he were killed for a slave, he would be equal to the slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and by the rest of the texts we have recited. Furthermore, his own slave is killed in retribution for his own slave. Therefore the slave of another must be equal to his own slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by these very texts we have cited. On this assumption, his own slave is equal to the slave of another in the meanings that necessitate retribution, so his own slave is a like of the like of himself, and the like of a like is a like. Therefore it is required that his own slave be a like of himself in the meanings that necessitate retribution. If a free person were killed for the slave of another, he would be killing himself by the explanation we have given, and he is not killed for his own slave. Therefore he must not be killed for the slave of another.

We have mentioned these ten examples as derivations from this verse. Whoever is guided by discernment will find it easy to derive many of the matters of the Sharia from this principle. And Allah knows best.

Here there is a discussion. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the cutting of hands: There is no doubt that all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of them or some of them. However, it is not possible to secure that right except by taking more than the equal, because the loss of ten hands is greater than the loss of one hand. Therefore it must remain under the original prohibition. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If the loss of ten hands in return for one hand were forbidden, then the loss of ten lives in return for one life would be forbidden, because the loss of a life includes the loss of a hand. So if the loss of ten hands in return for one hand is forbidden, then the loss of ten lives for one life includes what is forbidden. Whatever includes what is forbidden is itself forbidden. Thus the killing of ten lives in return for one life ought to be forbidden. Since we are agreed that it is not forbidden, we know that what you mentioned about taking more than the equal is not prohibited by the Sharia. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: We have made clear that His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, requires the observance of equivalence absolutely, in all circumstances, except in what the evidence has specified. The jurists have introduced specification into it in many cases, sometimes based on another text inferior to it, and sometimes based on analogy (qiyas). There is no doubt that whoever claims specification bears the burden of proof. The responsible person is sufficient to hold to this text in all claims. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: If he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," then he may say to him, "May Allah disgrace you." But if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then he does not have that right; rather, the prescribed punishment is what Allah has commanded.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, between himself and his adversary, through pardon and overlooking, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. ﴿His reward is with Allah﴾: this is a general promise whose matter is not measured in greatness.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: The purpose of it is to draw attention to the fact that the wronged party is not permitted to take more than the equal from the wrongdoer, because the wrongdoer, beyond his own wrongdoing, is protected. Self-defence is hardly secure from exceeding the equal and from transgression, especially in the state of war and the flaring up of zeal. Thus the wronged person may, at the time of proceeding to take retribution, become a wrongdoer. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: Whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand up." He said:
[p. 156]
Then a group will stand up, and it will be said to them: "What is your reward with Allah?" They will say: "We are the ones who pardoned those who wronged us." It will be said to them: "Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah, the Exalted."

**Second point:** When Allah, exalted is He, urged forgiveness of the wrongdoer, He informed that, despite this, He does not love him. This is a reminder that if He does not love such a person, yet it is still recommended to pardon him, then the believer, who is the beloved of Allah by virtue of his faith, is more deserving of pardoning him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, meaning after the wrongdoer's injustice toward him. This is an instance of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. ﴿Those—there is no blame upon them﴾, meaning the ones who defend themselves, ﴿no blame upon them﴾ such as punishment or censure, because they have acted in accordance with what was permitted to them of retaliation (intisar).

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse to demonstrate that the consequential harm (sirayah) of retaliatory punishment (qawad) is not liable. He said: The Law either says that He permitted him to cut [the offender] absolutely, or on the condition that no consequential harm results from it. The second is invalid, because the original ruling concerning cutting is prohibition. So if the permission to cut is conditioned on the absence of consequential harm, and this condition is unknown, that cutting must remain under the original ruling of prohibition, because the original ruling concerning it is prohibition, and permissibility is achieved only when it is conditioned on an unknown condition. Therefore it must remain under the original ruling of prohibition. Since this is not the case, we know that the Law permitted him to cut in whatever manner it occurs, whether harm results or not. If that is so, then that consequential harm must not be liable, because he has defended himself after being wronged. Therefore no one may have any blame upon him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾, meaning those who begin the injustice, ﴿and transgress in the earth without right. For them is a painful punishment.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ The meaning: ﴿And whoever is patient﴾ by not seeking retribution, ﴿and forgives﴾ and overlooks, ﴿indeed, that﴾ patience and overlooking ﴿is of the matters requiring determination﴾, meaning that his resolve to abandon retaliation is among the commendable matters requiring determination. The returning pronoun has been omitted because it is understood, just as it is omitted in the saying "ghee is two manns for a dirham." It is narrated that a man reviled another man in the gathering of al-Hasan, and the one being reviled kept silent, perspiring, and wiping off his sweat. Then he stood up and recited this verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it, and comprehended it, when the ignorant had neglected it."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him.﴾ That is, there is no helper for him who can take charge of him after his abandonment, meaning after Allah has led him astray. This is explicit in permitting that Allah, exalted is He, leads astray, and that guidance is not within the power of anyone other than Allah, exalted is He. The Qadi said: The intended meaning is: whoever Allah leads astray from Paradise, for him there is no protector after Him to help him. The response: restricting misguidance to this specific form is contrary to the evidence. Moreover, Allah did not lead him astray from Paradise according to your view; rather, he led himself astray from Paradise.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ The meaning is that they seek to return to the world because of the enormity of the punishment they witness. Then He mentioned their condition when the Fire is presented to them, saying: ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled from abasement﴾, meaning while they are humbled, debased, and disgraced because of the humiliation that has befallen them. Then He said: ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾, meaning their gaze begins with a faint, hidden movement of the eyelids, stealthily, like one who is certain to be killed looking at the sword: he looks at it as though he cannot open his eyelids upon it and fill his eyes with it, as he does when looking at beloved things.

If it is said: Did He not say, describing the disbelievers, that they will be gathered blind? How then does He say here that they look with a furtive glance? We say: Perhaps they are like this at the beginning and then are made blind; or perhaps this applies to one group, and that to another.

When Allah described the condition of the disbelievers, He related what the believers say about them, saying: ﴿And those who believe will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "On the Day of Resurrection" may either be connected to "lost", or the statement of the believers may be occurring in this world; or it may be connected to "said", meaning: they will say on the Day of Resurrection when they see them in that condition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment.﴾ That is, enduring. The Qadi said: This indicates that the disbeliever and the sinner will have their punishment endure. The response: the unqualified term "wrongdoer" in the Qur'an is specific to the disbeliever. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers.﴾ What confirms this is that He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿And they will have no protectors to help them besides Allah.﴾ The meaning is that the idols they worshipped in the hope that they would intercede for them with Allah, exalted is He, did not bring that intercession. It is known that this applies only to the disbelievers. Then He said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ This indicates that the one who misguides and the one who guides is Allah, exalted is He, according to what is our statement and our school of thought. And Allah knows best.

[p. 157]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 40–48 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And whoever avenges himself after being wronged, those—there is no blame upon them.﴾ ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right. Those will have a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ ﴿And you will see them exposed to it, humbled from disgrace, looking with sidelong glances. And those who believed will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers will be in lasting punishment."﴾ ﴿And they will have no protectors to support them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And those who, when tyranny strikes them, they defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 39], He followed it with what indicates that this self-defence must be restricted to an equal measure, for deficiency is injustice, excess is oppression, and equality is justice, by which the heavens and the earth stand. For this reason He said, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: One may say, "The retaliation for an evil is legislated and permitted, so how is it called an evil?" The author of al-Kashshaf answered this: both acts are called by the same name; the first deed, and its recompense, is an evil because it harms the one upon whom it falls. He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [al-Nisa: 78], meaning what displeases them of calamities and afflictions. Others answered that when one of the two was placed opposite the other, by way of metaphor, the name of one was applied to the other. The truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

The second issue: This verse is a great foundation in the science of jurisprudence (fiqh, the science of legal rulings derived from the sources). Its implication is that every offence should be met with its like. This is because leaving aggression unchecked opens the door to evil and transgression, since injustice, oppression and aggression are in the nature of every person. If he is not restrained from it, he will proceed with it and not abandon it. As for exceeding the measure of the offence, that is injustice, and the Sharia is free of it. Thus there remains only that it be met with an equal. Then this text was reinforced by other texts, such as His saying, ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿Prescribed for you is retribution for the murdered﴾ [al-Baqara: 178]. Retribution (qisas, the principle of equal retaliation) is an expression of equality and parity. His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45], and His saying, ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾ [al-Baqara: 179]. All these texts together require the requiting of a thing with its like.

Then here is a subtle point: when the right cannot be secured except by taking more than the equal, a conflict arises between inflicting additional harm on the offender and preventing the wronged party from securing his right. Which takes precedence? This is the place of the effort of the jurists (ijtihad), and this differs according to the different cases. Some matters have been derived from this principle, as a reminder of the rest.

The first example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that a Muslim is not killed for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection), and a free person is not killed for a slave, saying: Equivalence is a condition for the application of retribution, and it is absent in these two cases, so retribution must not apply between them. As for proving that equivalence is a condition for retribution, it is the texts mentioned, and the way to argue from them is this: either we take the equivalence mentioned in these texts as equivalence in all matters except what the evidence has specified, or we take it as equivalence in one specific matter. The second is weaker, because that specific matter is not mentioned in the verse, so if we read the verse as referring to it, it would entail ambiguity; and if we read the text as referring to the first sense, it would entail specification (takhsis, restricting a general text). It is known that removing ambiguity takes precedence over removing specification. So it is established that the verse requires observing equivalence in all matters, except what is specified by rational proof and by a separate textual proof. Given this, we say: observing equivalence in the killing of a Muslim for a dhimmi, and in the killing of a free person for a slave, is not possible, because Islam is regarded by the Sharia in imposing execution, either to establish it when it is absent, as in the case of an original disbeliever, or to preserve it when it is present, as in the case of an apostate. Also, freedom is a quality that the Sharia regards for judgeship, leadership, and testimony. Thus it is established that equivalence is a condition for the application of retribution, and it is absent here, so retribution must be prevented.

The second example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that hands are cut off for a single hand. He said: There is no doubt that when all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of those who cut, or from some of them, then it is required that the same be legislated against those cutters, by these texts. Whoever says that cutting is legislated, either in whole or in part, against all of them or some of them, has said that it is obligatory upon all. It remains to be said that this would entail taking more than the equal from the offender, which is forbidden. However, we say: when a conflict arose between the side of the offender and the side of the wronged party, the side of the wronged party takes precedence in consideration.

The third example: The partner of a father (in killing his child) is subject to retribution, and the proof of this is that the wounding proceeded from him, so he must be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾. When this is established, the full retribution is established too, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The fourth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever burns (someone), we burn him, and whoever drowns (someone), we drown him. The proof for this is these texts indicating the requiting of each thing with its like.

The fifth example: The witnesses in a retribution case, if they recant and say, "We deliberately lied," they are liable to retribution, because by that testimony they caused the blood of the accused to be wasted. Therefore their blood must become wasted, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The sixth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The one who is coerced is liable to retribution, because killing proceeded from him unjustly, so it is required that a like be imposed upon him. As for killing proceeding from him, the senses indicate it. As for its being unjust, that is because the Muslims unanimously agreed that he is charged by Allah, the Exalted, not to kill, and they unanimously agreed that by it he deserves a great sin and severe punishment. Given this, it is required that he be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The seventh example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Killing with a blunt object requires retribution. The proof for this is that the offender nullified his life, so the guardian of the one killed must be enabled to nullify the life of the killer, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The eighth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution. Although we mentioned this issue in the first example, we mention here another way of explanation. We say: the killer destroyed for the owner of the slave something worth, for instance, ten dinars. Therefore he is obliged to pay ten dinars, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And when compensation becomes obligatory, retribution must not become obligatory, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The ninth example: The usufruct of usurped property is liable to compensation according to Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The proof for this is that the usurper caused the owner to lose benefits that by custom are valued at one dinar. Therefore he must cause the usurper to lose a like amount of property, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And whoever requires that this amount be lost by the usurper also says that it must be paid to the one from whom it was usurped.

The tenth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution, because if he were killed for a slave, he would be equal to the slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and by the rest of the texts we have recited. Furthermore, his own slave is killed in retribution for his own slave. Therefore the slave of another must be equal to his own slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by these very texts we have cited. On this assumption, his own slave is equal to the slave of another in the meanings that necessitate retribution, so his own slave is a like of the like of himself, and the like of a like is a like. Therefore it is required that his own slave be a like of himself in the meanings that necessitate retribution. If a free person were killed for the slave of another, he would be killing himself by the explanation we have given, and he is not killed for his own slave. Therefore he must not be killed for the slave of another.

We have mentioned these ten examples as derivations from this verse. Whoever is guided by discernment will find it easy to derive many of the matters of the Sharia from this principle. And Allah knows best.

Here there is a discussion. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the cutting of hands: There is no doubt that all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of them or some of them. However, it is not possible to secure that right except by taking more than the equal, because the loss of ten hands is greater than the loss of one hand. Therefore it must remain under the original prohibition. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If the loss of ten hands in return for one hand were forbidden, then the loss of ten lives in return for one life would be forbidden, because the loss of a life includes the loss of a hand. So if the loss of ten hands in return for one hand is forbidden, then the loss of ten lives for one life includes what is forbidden. Whatever includes what is forbidden is itself forbidden. Thus the killing of ten lives in return for one life ought to be forbidden. Since we are agreed that it is not forbidden, we know that what you mentioned about taking more than the equal is not prohibited by the Sharia. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: We have made clear that His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, requires the observance of equivalence absolutely, in all circumstances, except in what the evidence has specified. The jurists have introduced specification into it in many cases, sometimes based on another text inferior to it, and sometimes based on analogy (qiyas). There is no doubt that whoever claims specification bears the burden of proof. The responsible person is sufficient to hold to this text in all claims. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: If he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," then he may say to him, "May Allah disgrace you." But if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then he does not have that right; rather, the prescribed punishment is what Allah has commanded.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, between himself and his adversary, through pardon and overlooking, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. ﴿His reward is with Allah﴾: this is a general promise whose matter is not measured in greatness.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: The purpose of it is to draw attention to the fact that the wronged party is not permitted to take more than the equal from the wrongdoer, because the wrongdoer, beyond his own wrongdoing, is protected. Self-defence is hardly secure from exceeding the equal and from transgression, especially in the state of war and the flaring up of zeal. Thus the wronged person may, at the time of proceeding to take retribution, become a wrongdoer. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: Whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand up." He said:
[p. 156]
Then a group will stand up, and it will be said to them: "What is your reward with Allah?" They will say: "We are the ones who pardoned those who wronged us." It will be said to them: "Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah, the Exalted."

**Second point:** When Allah, exalted is He, urged forgiveness of the wrongdoer, He informed that, despite this, He does not love him. This is a reminder that if He does not love such a person, yet it is still recommended to pardon him, then the believer, who is the beloved of Allah by virtue of his faith, is more deserving of pardoning him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, meaning after the wrongdoer's injustice toward him. This is an instance of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. ﴿Those—there is no blame upon them﴾, meaning the ones who defend themselves, ﴿no blame upon them﴾ such as punishment or censure, because they have acted in accordance with what was permitted to them of retaliation (intisar).

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse to demonstrate that the consequential harm (sirayah) of retaliatory punishment (qawad) is not liable. He said: The Law either says that He permitted him to cut [the offender] absolutely, or on the condition that no consequential harm results from it. The second is invalid, because the original ruling concerning cutting is prohibition. So if the permission to cut is conditioned on the absence of consequential harm, and this condition is unknown, that cutting must remain under the original ruling of prohibition, because the original ruling concerning it is prohibition, and permissibility is achieved only when it is conditioned on an unknown condition. Therefore it must remain under the original ruling of prohibition. Since this is not the case, we know that the Law permitted him to cut in whatever manner it occurs, whether harm results or not. If that is so, then that consequential harm must not be liable, because he has defended himself after being wronged. Therefore no one may have any blame upon him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾, meaning those who begin the injustice, ﴿and transgress in the earth without right. For them is a painful punishment.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ The meaning: ﴿And whoever is patient﴾ by not seeking retribution, ﴿and forgives﴾ and overlooks, ﴿indeed, that﴾ patience and overlooking ﴿is of the matters requiring determination﴾, meaning that his resolve to abandon retaliation is among the commendable matters requiring determination. The returning pronoun has been omitted because it is understood, just as it is omitted in the saying "ghee is two manns for a dirham." It is narrated that a man reviled another man in the gathering of al-Hasan, and the one being reviled kept silent, perspiring, and wiping off his sweat. Then he stood up and recited this verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it, and comprehended it, when the ignorant had neglected it."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him.﴾ That is, there is no helper for him who can take charge of him after his abandonment, meaning after Allah has led him astray. This is explicit in permitting that Allah, exalted is He, leads astray, and that guidance is not within the power of anyone other than Allah, exalted is He. The Qadi said: The intended meaning is: whoever Allah leads astray from Paradise, for him there is no protector after Him to help him. The response: restricting misguidance to this specific form is contrary to the evidence. Moreover, Allah did not lead him astray from Paradise according to your view; rather, he led himself astray from Paradise.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ The meaning is that they seek to return to the world because of the enormity of the punishment they witness. Then He mentioned their condition when the Fire is presented to them, saying: ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled from abasement﴾, meaning while they are humbled, debased, and disgraced because of the humiliation that has befallen them. Then He said: ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾, meaning their gaze begins with a faint, hidden movement of the eyelids, stealthily, like one who is certain to be killed looking at the sword: he looks at it as though he cannot open his eyelids upon it and fill his eyes with it, as he does when looking at beloved things.

If it is said: Did He not say, describing the disbelievers, that they will be gathered blind? How then does He say here that they look with a furtive glance? We say: Perhaps they are like this at the beginning and then are made blind; or perhaps this applies to one group, and that to another.

When Allah described the condition of the disbelievers, He related what the believers say about them, saying: ﴿And those who believe will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "On the Day of Resurrection" may either be connected to "lost", or the statement of the believers may be occurring in this world; or it may be connected to "said", meaning: they will say on the Day of Resurrection when they see them in that condition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment.﴾ That is, enduring. The Qadi said: This indicates that the disbeliever and the sinner will have their punishment endure. The response: the unqualified term "wrongdoer" in the Qur'an is specific to the disbeliever. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers.﴾ What confirms this is that He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿And they will have no protectors to help them besides Allah.﴾ The meaning is that the idols they worshipped in the hope that they would intercede for them with Allah, exalted is He, did not bring that intercession. It is known that this applies only to the disbelievers. Then He said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ This indicates that the one who misguides and the one who guides is Allah, exalted is He, according to what is our statement and our school of thought. And Allah knows best.

[p. 157]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 40–48 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And whoever avenges himself after being wronged, those—there is no blame upon them.﴾ ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress upon the earth without right. Those will have a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him. And you will see the wrongdoers when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ ﴿And you will see them exposed to it, humbled from disgrace, looking with sidelong glances. And those who believed will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who have lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers will be in lasting punishment."﴾ ﴿And they will have no protectors to support them against Allah. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And those who, when tyranny strikes them, they defend themselves﴾ [al-Shura: 39], He followed it with what indicates that this self-defence must be restricted to an equal measure, for deficiency is injustice, excess is oppression, and equality is justice, by which the heavens and the earth stand. For this reason He said, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: One may say, "The retaliation for an evil is legislated and permitted, so how is it called an evil?" The author of al-Kashshaf answered this: both acts are called by the same name; the first deed, and its recompense, is an evil because it harms the one upon whom it falls. He, the Exalted, said, ﴿And if an evil befalls them, they say, "This is from you [O Muhammad]"﴾ [al-Nisa: 78], meaning what displeases them of calamities and afflictions. Others answered that when one of the two was placed opposite the other, by way of metaphor, the name of one was applied to the other. The truth is what the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned.

The second issue: This verse is a great foundation in the science of jurisprudence (fiqh, the science of legal rulings derived from the sources). Its implication is that every offence should be met with its like. This is because leaving aggression unchecked opens the door to evil and transgression, since injustice, oppression and aggression are in the nature of every person. If he is not restrained from it, he will proceed with it and not abandon it. As for exceeding the measure of the offence, that is injustice, and the Sharia is free of it. Thus there remains only that it be met with an equal. Then this text was reinforced by other texts, such as His saying, ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished﴾ [al-Nahl: 126], His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿Prescribed for you is retribution for the murdered﴾ [al-Baqara: 178]. Retribution (qisas, the principle of equal retaliation) is an expression of equality and parity. His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45], and His saying, ﴿And for you in retribution is life﴾ [al-Baqara: 179]. All these texts together require the requiting of a thing with its like.

Then here is a subtle point: when the right cannot be secured except by taking more than the equal, a conflict arises between inflicting additional harm on the offender and preventing the wronged party from securing his right. Which takes precedence? This is the place of the effort of the jurists (ijtihad), and this differs according to the different cases. Some matters have been derived from this principle, as a reminder of the rest.

The first example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that a Muslim is not killed for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under Muslim protection), and a free person is not killed for a slave, saying: Equivalence is a condition for the application of retribution, and it is absent in these two cases, so retribution must not apply between them. As for proving that equivalence is a condition for retribution, it is the texts mentioned, and the way to argue from them is this: either we take the equivalence mentioned in these texts as equivalence in all matters except what the evidence has specified, or we take it as equivalence in one specific matter. The second is weaker, because that specific matter is not mentioned in the verse, so if we read the verse as referring to it, it would entail ambiguity; and if we read the text as referring to the first sense, it would entail specification (takhsis, restricting a general text). It is known that removing ambiguity takes precedence over removing specification. So it is established that the verse requires observing equivalence in all matters, except what is specified by rational proof and by a separate textual proof. Given this, we say: observing equivalence in the killing of a Muslim for a dhimmi, and in the killing of a free person for a slave, is not possible, because Islam is regarded by the Sharia in imposing execution, either to establish it when it is absent, as in the case of an original disbeliever, or to preserve it when it is present, as in the case of an apostate. Also, freedom is a quality that the Sharia regards for judgeship, leadership, and testimony. Thus it is established that equivalence is a condition for the application of retribution, and it is absent here, so retribution must be prevented.

The second example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, argued that hands are cut off for a single hand. He said: There is no doubt that when all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of those who cut, or from some of them, then it is required that the same be legislated against those cutters, by these texts. Whoever says that cutting is legislated, either in whole or in part, against all of them or some of them, has said that it is obligatory upon all. It remains to be said that this would entail taking more than the equal from the offender, which is forbidden. However, we say: when a conflict arose between the side of the offender and the side of the wronged party, the side of the wronged party takes precedence in consideration.

The third example: The partner of a father (in killing his child) is subject to retribution, and the proof of this is that the wounding proceeded from him, so he must be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And for wounds is retribution﴾. When this is established, the full retribution is established too, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The fourth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Whoever burns (someone), we burn him, and whoever drowns (someone), we drown him. The proof for this is these texts indicating the requiting of each thing with its like.

The fifth example: The witnesses in a retribution case, if they recant and say, "We deliberately lied," they are liable to retribution, because by that testimony they caused the blood of the accused to be wasted. Therefore their blood must become wasted, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The sixth example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The one who is coerced is liable to retribution, because killing proceeded from him unjustly, so it is required that a like be imposed upon him. As for killing proceeding from him, the senses indicate it. As for its being unjust, that is because the Muslims unanimously agreed that he is charged by Allah, the Exalted, not to kill, and they unanimously agreed that by it he deserves a great sin and severe punishment. Given this, it is required that he be requited with its like, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The seventh example: Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Killing with a blunt object requires retribution. The proof for this is that the offender nullified his life, so the guardian of the one killed must be enabled to nullify the life of the killer, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

The eighth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution. Although we mentioned this issue in the first example, we mention here another way of explanation. We say: the killer destroyed for the owner of the slave something worth, for instance, ten dinars. Therefore he is obliged to pay ten dinars, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And when compensation becomes obligatory, retribution must not become obligatory, because there is no one who distinguishes between them.

The ninth example: The usufruct of usurped property is liable to compensation according to Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. The proof for this is that the usurper caused the owner to lose benefits that by custom are valued at one dinar. Therefore he must cause the usurper to lose a like amount of property, by His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. And whoever requires that this amount be lost by the usurper also says that it must be paid to the one from whom it was usurped.

The tenth example: A free person is not killed for a slave in retribution, because if he were killed for a slave, he would be equal to the slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by His saying, ﴿Whoever does an evil will not be recompensed except with its like﴾ [Ghafir: 40], and by the rest of the texts we have recited. Furthermore, his own slave is killed in retribution for his own slave. Therefore the slave of another must be equal to his own slave in the meanings that necessitate retribution, by these very texts we have cited. On this assumption, his own slave is equal to the slave of another in the meanings that necessitate retribution, so his own slave is a like of the like of himself, and the like of a like is a like. Therefore it is required that his own slave be a like of himself in the meanings that necessitate retribution. If a free person were killed for the slave of another, he would be killing himself by the explanation we have given, and he is not killed for his own slave. Therefore he must not be killed for the slave of another.

We have mentioned these ten examples as derivations from this verse. Whoever is guided by discernment will find it easy to derive many of the matters of the Sharia from this principle. And Allah knows best.

Here there is a discussion. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the cutting of hands: There is no doubt that all of the cutting, or part of it, proceeded from all of them or some of them. However, it is not possible to secure that right except by taking more than the equal, because the loss of ten hands is greater than the loss of one hand. Therefore it must remain under the original prohibition. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: If the loss of ten hands in return for one hand were forbidden, then the loss of ten lives in return for one life would be forbidden, because the loss of a life includes the loss of a hand. So if the loss of ten hands in return for one hand is forbidden, then the loss of ten lives for one life includes what is forbidden. Whatever includes what is forbidden is itself forbidden. Thus the killing of ten lives in return for one life ought to be forbidden. Since we are agreed that it is not forbidden, we know that what you mentioned about taking more than the equal is not prohibited by the Sharia. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: We have made clear that His saying, ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾, requires the observance of equivalence absolutely, in all circumstances, except in what the evidence has specified. The jurists have introduced specification into it in many cases, sometimes based on another text inferior to it, and sometimes based on analogy (qiyas). There is no doubt that whoever claims specification bears the burden of proof. The responsible person is sufficient to hold to this text in all claims. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: If he says to him, "May Allah disgrace you," then he may say to him, "May Allah disgrace you." But if he slanders him in a way that requires the prescribed punishment (hadd), then he does not have that right; rather, the prescribed punishment is what Allah has commanded.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿But whoever pardons and makes reconciliation﴾, between himself and his adversary, through pardon and overlooking, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. ﴿His reward is with Allah﴾: this is a general promise whose matter is not measured in greatness.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wrongdoers﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: The purpose of it is to draw attention to the fact that the wronged party is not permitted to take more than the equal from the wrongdoer, because the wrongdoer, beyond his own wrongdoing, is protected. Self-defence is hardly secure from exceeding the equal and from transgression, especially in the state of war and the flaring up of zeal. Thus the wronged person may, at the time of proceeding to take retribution, become a wrongdoer. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the Day of Resurrection comes, a caller will call out: Whoever has a reward with Allah, let him stand up." He said:
[p. 156]
Then a group will stand up, and it will be said to them: "What is your reward with Allah?" They will say: "We are the ones who pardoned those who wronged us." It will be said to them: "Enter Paradise by the permission of Allah, the Exalted."

**Second point:** When Allah, exalted is He, urged forgiveness of the wrongdoer, He informed that, despite this, He does not love him. This is a reminder that if He does not love such a person, yet it is still recommended to pardon him, then the believer, who is the beloved of Allah by virtue of his faith, is more deserving of pardoning him.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever defends himself after being wronged﴾, meaning after the wrongdoer's injustice toward him. This is an instance of the verbal noun being annexed to its object. ﴿Those—there is no blame upon them﴾, meaning the ones who defend themselves, ﴿no blame upon them﴾ such as punishment or censure, because they have acted in accordance with what was permitted to them of retaliation (intisar).

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, used this verse to demonstrate that the consequential harm (sirayah) of retaliatory punishment (qawad) is not liable. He said: The Law either says that He permitted him to cut [the offender] absolutely, or on the condition that no consequential harm results from it. The second is invalid, because the original ruling concerning cutting is prohibition. So if the permission to cut is conditioned on the absence of consequential harm, and this condition is unknown, that cutting must remain under the original ruling of prohibition, because the original ruling concerning it is prohibition, and permissibility is achieved only when it is conditioned on an unknown condition. Therefore it must remain under the original ruling of prohibition. Since this is not the case, we know that the Law permitted him to cut in whatever manner it occurs, whether harm results or not. If that is so, then that consequential harm must not be liable, because he has defended himself after being wronged. Therefore no one may have any blame upon him.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people﴾, meaning those who begin the injustice, ﴿and transgress in the earth without right. For them is a painful punishment.﴾

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives—indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ The meaning: ﴿And whoever is patient﴾ by not seeking retribution, ﴿and forgives﴾ and overlooks, ﴿indeed, that﴾ patience and overlooking ﴿is of the matters requiring determination﴾, meaning that his resolve to abandon retaliation is among the commendable matters requiring determination. The returning pronoun has been omitted because it is understood, just as it is omitted in the saying "ghee is two manns for a dirham." It is narrated that a man reviled another man in the gathering of al-Hasan, and the one being reviled kept silent, perspiring, and wiping off his sweat. Then he stood up and recited this verse. Al-Hasan said: "By Allah, he understood it, and comprehended it, when the ignorant had neglected it."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no protector after Him.﴾ That is, there is no helper for him who can take charge of him after his abandonment, meaning after Allah has led him astray. This is explicit in permitting that Allah, exalted is He, leads astray, and that guidance is not within the power of anyone other than Allah, exalted is He. The Qadi said: The intended meaning is: whoever Allah leads astray from Paradise, for him there is no protector after Him to help him. The response: restricting misguidance to this specific form is contrary to the evidence. Moreover, Allah did not lead him astray from Paradise according to your view; rather, he led himself astray from Paradise.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you will see the wrongdoers, when they see the punishment, saying, "Is there any way to return?"﴾ The meaning is that they seek to return to the world because of the enormity of the punishment they witness. Then He mentioned their condition when the Fire is presented to them, saying: ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled from abasement﴾, meaning while they are humbled, debased, and disgraced because of the humiliation that has befallen them. Then He said: ﴿They look with a furtive glance﴾, meaning their gaze begins with a faint, hidden movement of the eyelids, stealthily, like one who is certain to be killed looking at the sword: he looks at it as though he cannot open his eyelids upon it and fill his eyes with it, as he does when looking at beloved things.

If it is said: Did He not say, describing the disbelievers, that they will be gathered blind? How then does He say here that they look with a furtive glance? We say: Perhaps they are like this at the beginning and then are made blind; or perhaps this applies to one group, and that to another.
