When Allah described the condition of the disbelievers, He related what the believers say about them, saying: ﴿And those who believe will say, "Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: "On the Day of Resurrection" may either be connected to "lost", or the statement of the believers may be occurring in this world; or it may be connected to "said", meaning: they will say on the Day of Resurrection when they see them in that condition.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Unquestionably, the wrongdoers are in lasting punishment.﴾ That is, enduring. The Qadi said: This indicates that the disbeliever and the sinner will have their punishment endure. The response: the unqualified term "wrongdoer" in the Qur'an is specific to the disbeliever. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers.﴾ What confirms this is that He, exalted is He, said after it: ﴿And they will have no protectors to help them besides Allah.﴾ The meaning is that the idols they worshipped in the hope that they would intercede for them with Allah, exalted is He, did not bring that intercession. It is known that this applies only to the disbelievers. Then He said: ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no way.﴾ This indicates that the one who misguides and the one who guides is Allah, exalted is He, according to what is our statement and our school of thought. And Allah knows best.

[p. 157]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 49–50:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day which there is no turning back from, from Allah. You will have no refuge that Day, nor will you have any denial﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to convey. And when We cause man to taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them for what their hands have sent forward, then indeed man is ungrateful﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows female offspring upon whom He wills, and He bestows male offspring upon whom He wills﴾ ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing, Competent﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had elaborated on the promise and the threat, He then mentioned what is the purpose, saying: ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day which there is no turning back from, from Allah﴾. His saying ﴿from Allah﴾ may be connected to His saying ﴿there is no turning back from﴾, meaning: Allah does not reverse it after He has decreed it. It may also be connected to His saying ﴿comes﴾, i.e., before there comes from Allah a Day which no one can avert. They differed about what is meant by that day. It was said: the day of the arrival of death. And it was said: the Day of Resurrection, because He described that day as ﴿there is no turning back from it﴾, and this description exists in both days. It is possible that the meaning of His saying ﴿there is no turning back from it﴾ is that it does not accept advancement or postponement, or that its meaning is that there is no return in it to the state of obligation so that there may be a making up (talafi).

Then Allah said, describing that day: ﴿You will have no refuge that day﴾ which saves from punishment, ﴿nor will you have any denial﴾ from anyone who would deny that, so that your state would change because of that denial. It is possible that the intended meaning of nakir is denial (inkar), i.e., you will not be able to deny anything of the deeds you have committed.

﴿But if they turn away﴾, i.e., these people to whom I commanded responding, i.e., they did not accept this command, ﴿We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ so that you would guard their deeds and count them, ﴿Your duty is only to convey﴾, and this is consolation from Allah, exalted is He. Then He explained the cause of their persistence in their false doctrines: they found in this world happiness and honour, and attainment of worldly aims produces arrogance, transgression, pride, and non-submission to the truth. So He said: ﴿And when We cause man to taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it﴾. The blessings of Allah in this world, although great, are compared to the blessings prepared in the Hereafter like a drop compared to the sea; therefore He named it "taste". Allah explained that when man succeeds in this paltry measure which he obtained in this world, he rejoices in it, his delusion grows because of it, and he falls into self-admiration and pride, and thinks that he has attained every wish and reached the furthest limits of happiness. This is the way of one whose belief in the happiness of the Hereafter is weak. This way is contrary to the way of the believer who does not regard the blessings of this world except as a means to the blessings of the Hereafter. Then He explained that whenever an ''evil'' befalls them, i.e., something that displeases them at the moment, such as illness, poverty and other things, then disbelief appears from them, and this is the meaning of His saying ﴿indeed man is ungrateful﴾. The kafur is one who is exaggerated in ingratitude. He did not say "indeed he is ungrateful", to show that the nature of man requires this state, unless a man disciplines it with the good manners to which Allah has guided.

When Allah mentioned man's being made to taste mercy and his being struck by its opposite, He followed that with His saying ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. The purpose of this is that man should not be deceived by the wealth and status he possesses, but rather, when he knows that all of it is Allah's ownership and dominion, and that he only obtained that measure under his hand because Allah bestowed it upon him, then that becomes a motive for him to greater obedience and service. But if he believes that those blessings come about through his own intellect, effort and diligence, he remains deceived by himself, turning away from the obedience of Allah, exalted is He. Then He mentioned, among the kinds of Allah's disposal of the world, that He specifies some with daughters, some with sons, some with both, and some by making them deprived of all, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾.

Know that the people of the natural sciences say: the cause of the birth of a child is the soundness of the state of the sperm and the womb; the cause of maleness is the predominance of heat; the cause of femaleness is the predominance of cold. We have mentioned this topic exhaustively in surah an-Nahl, and refuted it with certain proofs, and it became clear that this is from Allah, exalted is He, not from natures, stars and spheres. In the verse there are questions:

The first question: He placed females first in mention before males, saying ﴿He bestows female offspring upon whom He wills, and He bestows male offspring upon whom He wills﴾, then in the second verse He placed males before females, saying ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females﴾. What is the reason for this advancing and postponing?

The second question: He mentioned the females in the indefinite form, saying ﴿female offspring﴾, and mentioned the males with the definite form, saying ﴿the male offspring﴾. What is the reason for this distinction?

The third question: Why did He use the word "bestow" for giving females alone and for giving males alone, saying ﴿He bestows female offspring upon whom He wills, and He bestows male offspring upon whom He wills﴾, while for giving both categories together He said ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females﴾?

The fourth question: Since the occurrence of offspring is a gift from Allah, it would suffice for its non-occurrence that He not bestow it. What need is there, in the case of non-occurrence, for Him to say ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾?

The fifth question: Is the intended meaning of this ruling a specific group of people, or is the ruling about humanity in general?

The answer to the first question has several aspects:

First: the generous person strives that the conclusion be upon goodness, ease, joy and delight. So when a female child is given first and then a male after her, it is as if He moved him from grief to joy, and this is the utmost generosity. But if He gives a child first and then a female afterwards, it is as if He moved him from joy to grief. So He mentioned the gift of a female child first, and second the gift of a male child, so that He would have moved him from grief to joy, and that is more fitting to generosity.

The second aspect: when a female child is given first, he knows that he has no objection to Allah, exalted is He, and so he is content with that; then when He gives him a male child after that, he knows that this added increase is a bounty from Allah, exalted is He, and a kindness to him, so his gratitude and obedience increase, and he knows that this came about purely by grace and generosity.

The third aspect: some preachers have said: the female is weak, deficient, and incapable, so He mentioned her first to alert that the more complete the weakness and need, the greater Allah's care for it.

The fourth aspect: as if it were said: O weak, incapable woman, indeed your father and your mother dislike your existence. If they have disliked your existence, I have placed you first in mention so that you know that the one who is benevolent and honourable is Allah, exalted is He. When the woman knows that, she increases in obedience, service, and distance from the causes of reproach and blame. These are the meanings for which the mention of females was placed before the mention of males. And He placed the mention of males after the mention of females because the male is more complete and more excellent than the female, and the more excellent and more complete is placed before the baser and more contemptible. The conclusion is that considering it as male or female requires placing the mention of the male before the mention of the female, but the external accidents that we mentioned have required placing the mention of the female before the mention of the male. When the factor requiring advancement and postponement arose in both cases, He therefore placed this first once and that first another time. And Allah knows best.

As for the second question, which is His saying: why did He express the females with the indefinite form and the males with the definite form? Its answer is that the purpose of this is to alert to the fact that the male is more excellent than the female.

As for the third question, which is His saying: why did He say, exalted is He, regarding giving the two categories ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾? Its answer is that every two things that are joined one with the other are a pair (zawj), and each one of them is called a spouse (zawj). The pronoun in ﴿He pairs them﴾ refers to the females and males mentioned in the first verse, and the meaning is: He joins the females and males, making them pairs.

As for the fourth question, its answer is that the barren one (aqim) is the one who does not bear offspring. It is said: a barren man who does not beget, and a barren woman who does not bear. The root of ʿuqm is cutting, and from it it is said: "kingship is barren (ʿaqim)", because the ties of kinship are cut in it by killing and disobedience to parents.

As for the fifth question, its answer: Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿He bestows female offspring upon whom He wills﴾ means Lut and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, who had only daughters; ﴿and He bestows male offspring upon whom He wills﴾ means Ibrahim, peace be upon him, who had only sons; ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾ means Muhammad (ﷺ), who had four sons: al-Qasim, al-Tahir, Abdullah and Ibrahim, and four daughters: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah; ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ means Isa and Yahya. Most of the exegetes said: this ruling is general with regard to all people, because the purpose is to show the effectiveness of Allah's power in creating things as He wills and intends, so there was no sense in specification. And Allah knows best. Then He concluded the verse with His saying ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing, Competent﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Knowing of what He has created, Competent over what He wills to create. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 49–50:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day which there is no turning back from, from Allah. You will have no refuge that Day, nor will you have any denial﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a guardian over them. Your duty is only to convey. And when We cause man to taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it; but if an evil befalls them for what their hands have sent forward, then indeed man is ungrateful﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows female offspring upon whom He wills, and He bestows male offspring upon whom He wills﴾ ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing, Competent﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had elaborated on the promise and the threat, He then mentioned what is the purpose, saying: ﴿Respond to your Lord before there comes a Day which there is no turning back from, from Allah﴾. His saying ﴿from Allah﴾ may be connected to His saying ﴿there is no turning back from﴾, meaning: Allah does not reverse it after He has decreed it. It may also be connected to His saying ﴿comes﴾, i.e., before there comes from Allah a Day which no one can avert. They differed about what is meant by that day. It was said: the day of the arrival of death. And it was said: the Day of Resurrection, because He described that day as ﴿there is no turning back from it﴾, and this description exists in both days. It is possible that the meaning of His saying ﴿there is no turning back from it﴾ is that it does not accept advancement or postponement, or that its meaning is that there is no return in it to the state of obligation so that there may be a making up (talafi).

Then Allah said, describing that day: ﴿You will have no refuge that day﴾ which saves from punishment, ﴿nor will you have any denial﴾ from anyone who would deny that, so that your state would change because of that denial. It is possible that the intended meaning of nakir is denial (inkar), i.e., you will not be able to deny anything of the deeds you have committed.

﴿But if they turn away﴾, i.e., these people to whom I commanded responding, i.e., they did not accept this command, ﴿We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ so that you would guard their deeds and count them, ﴿Your duty is only to convey﴾, and this is consolation from Allah, exalted is He. Then He explained the cause of their persistence in their false doctrines: they found in this world happiness and honour, and attainment of worldly aims produces arrogance, transgression, pride, and non-submission to the truth. So He said: ﴿And when We cause man to taste mercy from Us, he rejoices in it﴾. The blessings of Allah in this world, although great, are compared to the blessings prepared in the Hereafter like a drop compared to the sea; therefore He named it "taste". Allah explained that when man succeeds in this paltry measure which he obtained in this world, he rejoices in it, his delusion grows because of it, and he falls into self-admiration and pride, and thinks that he has attained every wish and reached the furthest limits of happiness. This is the way of one whose belief in the happiness of the Hereafter is weak. This way is contrary to the way of the believer who does not regard the blessings of this world except as a means to the blessings of the Hereafter. Then He explained that whenever an ''evil'' befalls them, i.e., something that displeases them at the moment, such as illness, poverty and other things, then disbelief appears from them, and this is the meaning of His saying ﴿indeed man is ungrateful﴾. The kafur is one who is exaggerated in ingratitude. He did not say "indeed he is ungrateful", to show that the nature of man requires this state, unless a man disciplines it with the good manners to which Allah has guided.

When Allah mentioned man's being made to taste mercy and his being struck by its opposite, He followed that with His saying ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. The purpose of this is that man should not be deceived by the wealth and status he possesses, but rather, when he knows that all of it is Allah's ownership and dominion, and that he only obtained that measure under his hand because Allah bestowed it upon him, then that becomes a motive for him to greater obedience and service. But if he believes that those blessings come about through his own intellect, effort and diligence, he remains deceived by himself, turning away from the obedience of Allah, exalted is He. Then He mentioned, among the kinds of Allah's disposal of the world, that He specifies some with daughters, some with sons, some with both, and some by making them deprived of all, and this is what is meant by His saying ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾.

Know that the people of the natural sciences say: the cause of the birth of a child is the soundness of the state of the sperm and the womb; the cause of maleness is the predominance of heat; the cause of femaleness is the predominance of cold. We have mentioned this topic exhaustively in surah an-Nahl, and refuted it with certain proofs, and it became clear that this is from Allah, exalted is He, not from natures, stars and spheres. In the verse there are questions:

The first question: He placed females first in mention before males, saying ﴿He bestows female offspring upon whom He wills, and He bestows male offspring upon whom He wills﴾, then in the second verse He placed males before females, saying ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females﴾. What is the reason for this advancing and postponing?

The second question: He mentioned the females in the indefinite form, saying ﴿female offspring﴾, and mentioned the males with the definite form, saying ﴿the male offspring﴾. What is the reason for this distinction?

The third question: Why did He use the word "bestow" for giving females alone and for giving males alone, saying ﴿He bestows female offspring upon whom He wills, and He bestows male offspring upon whom He wills﴾, while for giving both categories together He said ﴿Or He pairs them, males and females﴾?

The fourth question: Since the occurrence of offspring is a gift from Allah, it would suffice for its non-occurrence that He not bestow it. What need is there, in the case of non-occurrence, for Him to say ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾?

The fifth question: Is the intended meaning of this ruling a specific group of people, or is the ruling about humanity in general?

The answer to the first question has several aspects:

First: the generous person strives that the conclusion be upon goodness, ease, joy and delight. So when a female child is given first and then a male after her, it is as if He moved him from grief to joy, and this is the utmost generosity. But if He gives a child first and then a female afterwards, it is as if He moved him from joy to grief. So He mentioned the gift of a female child first, and second the gift of a male child, so that He would have moved him from grief to joy, and that is more fitting to generosity.

The second aspect: when a female child is given first, he knows that he has no objection to Allah, exalted is He, and so he is content with that; then when He gives him a male child after that, he knows that this added increase is a bounty from Allah, exalted is He, and a kindness to him, so his gratitude and obedience increase, and he knows that this came about purely by grace and generosity.

The third aspect: some preachers have said: the female is weak, deficient, and incapable, so He mentioned her first to alert that the more complete the weakness and need, the greater Allah's care for it.

The fourth aspect: as if it were said: O weak, incapable woman, indeed your father and your mother dislike your existence. If they have disliked your existence, I have placed you first in mention so that you know that the one who is benevolent and honourable is Allah, exalted is He. When the woman knows that, she increases in obedience, service, and distance from the causes of reproach and blame. These are the meanings for which the mention of females was placed before the mention of males. And He placed the mention of males after the mention of females because the male is more complete and more excellent than the female, and the more excellent and more complete is placed before the baser and more contemptible. The conclusion is that considering it as male or female requires placing the mention of the male before the mention of the female, but the external accidents that we mentioned have required placing the mention of the female before the mention of the male. When the factor requiring advancement and postponement arose in both cases, He therefore placed this first once and that first another time. And Allah knows best.

As for the second question, which is His saying: why did He express the females with the indefinite form and the males with the definite form? Its answer is that the purpose of this is to alert to the fact that the male is more excellent than the female.

As for the third question, which is His saying: why did He say, exalted is He, regarding giving the two categories ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾? Its answer is that every two things that are joined one with the other are a pair (zawj), and each one of them is called a spouse (zawj). The pronoun in ﴿He pairs them﴾ refers to the females and males mentioned in the first verse, and the meaning is: He joins the females and males, making them pairs.

As for the fourth question, its answer is that the barren one (aqim) is the one who does not bear offspring. It is said: a barren man who does not beget, and a barren woman who does not bear. The root of ʿuqm is cutting, and from it it is said: "kingship is barren (ʿaqim)", because the ties of kinship are cut in it by killing and disobedience to parents.

As for the fifth question, its answer: Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿He bestows female offspring upon whom He wills﴾ means Lut and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, who had only daughters; ﴿and He bestows male offspring upon whom He wills﴾ means Ibrahim, peace be upon him, who had only sons; ﴿or He pairs them, males and females﴾ means Muhammad (ﷺ), who had four sons: al-Qasim, al-Tahir, Abdullah and Ibrahim, and four daughters: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah; ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ means Isa and Yahya. Most of the exegetes said: this ruling is general with regard to all people, because the purpose is to show the effectiveness of Allah's power in creating things as He wills and intends, so there was no sense in specification. And Allah knows best. Then He concluded the verse with His saying ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing, Competent﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Knowing of what He has created, Competent over what He wills to create. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 51–53 (part 1 of 2)**

**His saying, may He be exalted:** ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation (waḥy), or from behind a veil, or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills. Indeed He is Most High, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed you guide to a straight path.﴾ ﴿The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had shown the perfection of His power, knowledge and wisdom, He followed it with an explanation of how He singles out His prophets with His revelation and His speech. The verse contains several issues:

**First issue:** ﴿It is not for a human﴾, meaning it is not valid for any human, ﴿that Allah should speak to him﴾, except in one of three ways. The first is by revelation (waḥy), which is inspiration (ilhām) and a casting into the heart. Or it is by dream, as Allah revealed to the mother of Moses, and to Abraham, peace be upon him, concerning the slaughter of his son. It is also reported from Mujahid that Allah revealed the Psalms to David, peace be upon him, into his breast. The second way is that He makes him hear His speech without an intermediary messenger. This too is revelation, as evidenced by the fact that He made Moses hear His speech without an intermediary, and yet He called it revelation, in His saying: ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾. The third way is that He sends to him a messenger from among the angels, who conveys that revelation to the human messenger.

The method of delimitation is to say: the arrival of revelation from Allah to a human is either without an intermediary conveyor or through an intermediary conveyor. If it is the first, that revelation reaches him without another person, then here it is either said that he did not hear the very speech of Allah, or that he heard it. The first, that revelation reached him without another person and he did not hear the very speech of Allah, is what is meant by His saying ﴿except by revelation﴾.

The second, that revelation reached him without another person but he heard the very speech of Allah, is what is meant by His saying ﴿or from behind a veil﴾.

The third, that revelation reached him through another person, is what is meant by His saying ﴿or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾.

Know that each of these three categories is revelation, but He specified the first category with the name "revelation," because what falls into the heart by way of inspiration falls all at once, so it was more appropriate to restrict the word "revelation" to it. This is the discussion on distinguishing these categories from one another.

**Second issue:** Those who hold that Allah is in a place cite His saying ﴿or from behind a veil﴾. The reasoning is that the implied meaning is: "It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except in one of three ways:
One of them: that Allah be from behind a veil." This would only be valid if He were specific to a particular place and a particular direction.

The answer: although the apparent wording may suggest what you mention, the rational and transmitted proofs have indicated that He, exalted is He, cannot be in a place or a direction. Therefore this wording must be taken in a figurative interpretation (ta'wīl). The meaning is that when a man hears speech while not seeing the speaker, this resembles what happens when one speaks from behind a veil, and resemblance is a cause for the permissibility of metaphor (majāz).

[161]

**Third issue:** The Mu'tazila said: this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, cannot be seen, because He, exalted is He, has restricted the categories of His revelation to these three. If the seeing of Allah were valid, then it would be valid for Allah to speak with the servant at the time the servant sees Him, and then that would be a fourth category beyond these three. Allah, exalted is He, negated the fourth category by His saying ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him﴾, except in these three ways.

The answer: we add a qualifier to the wording, so the implied meaning becomes: "It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him in this world except in one of these three categories." In that case, what you have mentioned does not follow. Although adding this qualifier is contrary to the apparent meaning, it is necessary to resort to it in order to reconcile these verses with the verses indicating that vision will occur on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah knows best.

**Fourth issue:** The community (ummah) has agreed that Allah, exalted is He, is a speaker (mutakallim). Everyone other than the Ash'ariyya and their followers has unanimously held that the speech of Allah is these letters that are heard and these sounds that are composed. As for al-Ash'ari and his followers, they claimed that the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is an eternal attribute (ṣifa qadīma) that is expressed by these letters and sounds.

As for the first group, those who said that the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is these letters and words, they are two groups. One of them is the Hanbalites, who said that these letters are eternal. These people are too base to be mentioned among the intelligent. It happened one day that I said to some of them: If Allah spoke with these letters, He would either speak with them all at once, or in succession and sequence. The first is invalid, because speaking with the whole of these letters at once would not produce this composed arrangement in this sequence and succession. Therefore this composed arrangement of these successive letters would not be the speech of Allah, exalted is He. The second is also invalid, because if He spoke with them in succession and sequence, they would be originated (muḥdatha). When that man heard this argument, he said: "It is obligatory upon us to affirm (nuqirr) and to pass over (namurr)," meaning: we affirm that the Qur'an is eternal, and we pass over this speech according to what we heard. I was astonished at the soundness of that speaker's heart. As for the intelligent people, they have unanimously agreed that these letters and sounds come into existence after not having been, and become present after having been non-existent. Then their expressions differed as to whether they are created (makhlūq), or whether one should not say that, but rather say that they are originated (ḥādith), or express it in another wording. They also differed as to whether these letters subsist in the essence of Allah, exalted is He, or whether He creates them in another body. The first is the view of the Karramiyya, and the second is the view of the Mu'tazila.

As for the Ash'ariyya, who claimed that the speech of Allah is an eternal attribute indicated by these words and expressions, they agreed that His saying ﴿or from behind a veil﴾ means that the angel and the messenger hear that speech, which is exempt from letter and sound, from behind a veil. They said: just as it is not far-fetched that one sees the essence of Allah although He is not a body and not in a space, what is far-fetched about hearing the speech of Allah although it is not a letter and not a sound?

Abu Mansur al-Maturidi al-Samarqandi claimed that this subsisting attribute cannot be heard, and that what is heard is only letters and sounds that Allah, exalted is He, creates in the tree. This view is close to the view of the Mu'tazila. And Allah knows best.

**Fifth issue:** The Qadi said: this verse indicates the origination (ḥudūth) of the speech of Allah, exalted is He, in several respects:

First: His saying ﴿that Allah should speak to him﴾ indicates this, because the word ﴿an﴾ with the imperfect verb conveys the future.

Second: He described the speech as revelation, because the word "revelation" indicates that it occurred in the swiftest manner.

Third: His saying ﴿or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ requires that the speech which the angel conveys to the human messenger be like the speech he heard from Allah. What he conveys to the human messenger is originated. So when the speech he heard from Allah is similar to this which he conveyed to the human messenger, and this which he conveyed to the human messenger is originated, and the like of the originated is originated, it is necessary to say that the speech he heard from Allah is originated.

[162]

Fourth: His saying ﴿or that He sends a messenger and he reveals﴾ requires that the revelation occur after the sending, and whatever's occurrence is subsequent to the occurrence of something else is originated.

The answer: we redirect the whole of these aspects you have mentioned to the letters and sounds, and we acknowledge that they are originated, coming into existence after not having been. The self-evident intellect bears witness that the matter is so. So what need is there to establish this claimed point, whose soundness you know by the self-evident intellect and by the apparent meanings of the Qur'an? And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**Sixth issue:** It has been established that revelation from Allah, exalted is He, either does not occur through another person, and it is impossible that all revelation occurs through another person, for otherwise either an infinite regress (tasalsul) or circularity (dawr) would follow, and both are impossible. Therefore it is necessary to acknowledge that there is a revelation which occurs without another person. Then here are some discussions:

**First discussion:** The first person who heard the revelation of Allah without another person, how does he know that the speech he heard is the speech of Allah? If we say that he heard that eternal attribute, exempt from being a letter and a sound, it is not far-fetched that when he hears it he knows by necessity that it is the speech of Allah, exalted is He, and it is not far-fetched to say that he then needs an additional proof. But if we say that what is heard is the letter and the sound, it is impossible to be certain that it is the speech of Allah, exalted is He, unless a proof appears indicating that this heard thing is the speech of Allah, exalted is He.

**Second discussion:** When the messenger hears it from the angel, how does he know that this conveyor is a sinless angel and not a misguiding devil? The truth is that he cannot be certain of that except on the basis of a miracle (mu'jiza) indicating that this conveyor is a sinless angel and not an evil devil. On this basis, the revelation from Allah, exalted is He, is not completed except through three levels of the appearance of miracles:

The first level: when the angel hears that speech from Allah, exalted is He, there must be a miracle for him indicating that this speech is the speech of Allah, exalted is He.

The second level: when that angel reaches the messenger, there must also be a miracle for him.

The third level: when that messenger conveys it to the community, there must also be a miracle for him. Thus it is established that obligation does not fall upon creation except after the occurrence of three levels of miracles.

**Third discussion:** There is no doubt that an angel among the angels heard the revelation from Allah, exalted is He, at the outset. That angel is Gabriel (Jibril). It may be said: perhaps Gabriel heard it from another angel. All of these are possible, even through a thousand intermediaries, and nothing has been found that indicates certainty about any one of these possibilities.

**Fourth discussion:** Is there anyone among humans who heard the revelation of Allah, exalted is He, without an intermediary? It is well known that Moses, peace be upon him, heard the speech of Allah without an intermediary, based on His saying: ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾. It has also been said that Muhammad (ﷺ) heard it too, based on His saying: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10].

**Fifth discussion:** The angels are able to appear to people in different forms. So supposing that the Messenger (ﷺ) sees him each time, it would be necessary for him to need a miracle, so that he would know that the one he sees this time is the same as the one he saw the first time. And if he does not see his person, then the need for a miracle would be even stronger, because of the possibility that confusion occurred regarding the voice. However, the claim that a miracle must be shown every time has not been held by anyone.

[163]

**Seventh issue:** The disputations mentioned in the Qur'an between Allah, exalted is He, and Iblis indicate that He, exalted is He, was speaking with Iblis without an intermediary. Whether that is called revelation from Allah, exalted is He, to Iblis or not, the more apparent view is that it is not so called. And at this point there must be a complete and subtle discussion.

**The Eighth Issue:** Nafi' recited *"aw yursila rasulan"* (أَوْ يُرْسِلُ رَسُولًا) with a *raf'* (مرفوع) vowel on the *lam*, and *"fa-yuhiya"* (فَيُوحِي) with a sukun on the *ya'*. Its position is in the nominative case, on the assumption of the implied phrase: *"wa-huwa yursilu fa-yuhiya"* (and He sends, so He reveals). The rest of the readers recited it in the accusative (*nasb*), interpreting it as a verbal noun (*ta'wil al-masdar*), as if it were said: *"It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation (wahyan), or by making him hear His speech from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger."* However, there is a difficulty here: the phrase *wahyan aw isma'an* is a noun, while the phrase *"aw yursila"* is a verb, and coordinating a verb with a noun is considered weak. This was answered by saying that the intended meaning is: *"It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except that He reveal to him by revelation (illa an yuhiya ilayhi wahyan), or make him hear by making him hear (aw yusmi'a isma'an) from behind a veil, or send a messenger (aw yursila rasulan)."*

**The Ninth Issue:** According to the People of the Truth (Ahl al-Haqq), the correct view is that while the angel conveys the revelation to the Messenger, Satan cannot cast falsehood into the course of that revelation. Some have said that this is possible, citing the words of Allah the Exalted: *"We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he spoke, Satan cast into his wish"* (22:52). They also said that Satan cast, in the course of Surat al-Najm, *"Those are the exalted cranes, whose intercession is to be hoped for."* Our friend, the king Sam ibn Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, who was the most excellent of the men of authority I ever met, used to say: "This statement, after the strong and overpowering proofs, is false for two other reasons:"

*The first:* The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sees me in a dream has indeed seen me, for Satan cannot take on my form." If Satan cannot take on the form of the Messenger in a dream, how could he be able to imitate Jibril (Gabriel) at the time of conveying the revelation of Allah the Exalted?

*The second:* The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Umar never took a path except that Satan took another path." If Satan cannot be present with Umar on a single path, how could he be able to be present with Jibril at the moment of conveying the revelation of Allah the Exalted?

**The Tenth Issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted, *"so that he reveals by His permission what He wills"* (42:51), mean: that angel reveals, by the permission of Allah, what Allah wills. This implies that goodness is not good because of an attribute that returns to it, and that evil is not evil because of an attribute that returns to it. Rather, Allah may command whatever He wills without specification, and forbid whatever He wills without specification. For if the matter were not so, His saying "what He wills" would not be correct. And Allah knows best.

Then Allah the Exalted said at the end of the verse: *"Indeed He is Most High, All-Wise."* That is, He is exalted above the attributes of the created beings, and *"All-Wise"* means He carries out His acts in accordance with the requirements of wisdom. He speaks at times without an intermediary, by way of inspiration (ilham); at other times by making speech heard; and at a third time through the mediation of the noble angels. When Allah the Exalted explained the modes of revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them, He said: *"And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command"* (42:52). The intended meaning is the Qur'an, and He called it a *"spirit"* (ruh) because it gives life after the death of ignorance or disbelief.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: *"You did not know what the Book was, nor faith"* (42:52). The scholars differed concerning this verse, with a consensus (ijma') that it is not permissible to say that the messengers were upon disbelief before revelation. They mentioned several answers:

*First:* *"You did not know what the Book was"*, that is, the Qur'an, *"nor faith"*, that is, the prayer (salah), based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: *"And Allah would not let your faith go to waste"* (2:143), meaning your prayer. [Page 164]

*Second:* This is to be understood as an elision of a noun (hadhf al-mudaf). That is: *"You did not know what the Book was, nor who the people of faith were"*, meaning who believes and who does not believe.

*Third:* *"You did not know what the Book was, nor faith"* when you were a child in the cradle.

*Fourth:* "Faith" (iman) is an expression for affirming everything that Allah the Exalted has obligated. Before prophethood, he (ﷺ) was not acquainted with all of Allah's obligations, but he was acquainted with Allah the Exalted, and this does not contradict what we have mentioned.

*Fifth:* The attributes of Allah the Exalted are of two kinds. Some of them can be known by purely rational proofs, and others cannot be known except through revealed (sam'i) proofs. This second kind had not been known to him before prophethood.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: *"But We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* (42:52). They differed regarding the pronoun in His saying *"But We made it"*. Some said it refers to the Qur'an alone, not to faith, because it is by it that rulings are known; therefore it is rightly likened to the light by which one is guided. Others said it refers to both together, and this is acceptable because their meaning is one, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: *"And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush to it"* (62:11).

* * *

Then He said: *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants."* This indicates that, after He made the Qur'an itself a guidance in its own essence, as He said: *"guidance for the righteous"* (2:2), He may guide some by it and not others. And this guidance is nothing other than an expression for the call (da'wah) and the clarification of the proofs. For Allah the Exalted said of Muhammad (ﷺ): *"And indeed, you guide to a straight path"* (42:52), which conveys generality with respect to all. His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* conveys particularity. Thus it is established that guidance in the sense of the call is general, while the guidance in His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* is specific. The specific guidance is other than the general guidance. Therefore, what is meant by His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* must be something different from the manifestation of the proofs and the removal of excuses. It is also not permissible that it be an expression for guidance to the path of Paradise, because He said: *"But We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"*, that is, We made the Qur'an a light by which We guide whom We will. This befits only the guidance that occurs in this world. Furthermore, guidance to Paradise, according to you, is obligatory for some and forbidden for others, and on either assumption, His saying *"whom We will of Our servants"* would serve no purpose. Thus it is established that what is meant is that He guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, and there is no objection to Him in this.

Then Allah the Exalted said to Muhammad (ﷺ): *"And indeed, you guide to a straight path"* (42:52). He thus made clear that just as the Qur'an guides, so too the Messenger guides. And He made clear that he guides *"to a straight path"*, and He explained that this path is *"the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"* (42:53). By this He draws attention to the fact that the One who is worthy of worship is the One who owns the heavens and the earth. The purpose of this is to invalidate the claim of those who worship other than Allah.

* * *

Then He said: *"Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned"* (42:53). This is in the manner of a warning and a rebuke. He made clear that the affair of whoever does not accept these obligations returns to Allah the Exalted, that is, to where there is no judge other than Him, and He will recompense each of them with what they deserve of reward or punishment.

He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The commentary on this surah was completed on the last day of Friday, the eighth of the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, in the year six hundred and three. O Director of affairs, O Eternal Ruler of the ages, O Giver of every good and joy, O Repeller of trials and evils, bring us to the abodes of light, in the darkness of the graves, by Your grace and mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 42, verses 51–53 (part 1 of 2)**

**His saying, may He be exalted:** ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation (waḥy), or from behind a veil, or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills. Indeed He is Most High, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants. And indeed you guide to a straight path.﴾ ﴿The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had shown the perfection of His power, knowledge and wisdom, He followed it with an explanation of how He singles out His prophets with His revelation and His speech. The verse contains several issues:

**First issue:** ﴿It is not for a human﴾, meaning it is not valid for any human, ﴿that Allah should speak to him﴾, except in one of three ways. The first is by revelation (waḥy), which is inspiration (ilhām) and a casting into the heart. Or it is by dream, as Allah revealed to the mother of Moses, and to Abraham, peace be upon him, concerning the slaughter of his son. It is also reported from Mujahid that Allah revealed the Psalms to David, peace be upon him, into his breast. The second way is that He makes him hear His speech without an intermediary messenger. This too is revelation, as evidenced by the fact that He made Moses hear His speech without an intermediary, and yet He called it revelation, in His saying: ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾. The third way is that He sends to him a messenger from among the angels, who conveys that revelation to the human messenger.

The method of delimitation is to say: the arrival of revelation from Allah to a human is either without an intermediary conveyor or through an intermediary conveyor. If it is the first, that revelation reaches him without another person, then here it is either said that he did not hear the very speech of Allah, or that he heard it. The first, that revelation reached him without another person and he did not hear the very speech of Allah, is what is meant by His saying ﴿except by revelation﴾.

The second, that revelation reached him without another person but he heard the very speech of Allah, is what is meant by His saying ﴿or from behind a veil﴾.

The third, that revelation reached him through another person, is what is meant by His saying ﴿or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾.

Know that each of these three categories is revelation, but He specified the first category with the name "revelation," because what falls into the heart by way of inspiration falls all at once, so it was more appropriate to restrict the word "revelation" to it. This is the discussion on distinguishing these categories from one another.

**Second issue:** Those who hold that Allah is in a place cite His saying ﴿or from behind a veil﴾. The reasoning is that the implied meaning is: "It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except in one of three ways:
One of them: that Allah be from behind a veil." This would only be valid if He were specific to a particular place and a particular direction.

The answer: although the apparent wording may suggest what you mention, the rational and transmitted proofs have indicated that He, exalted is He, cannot be in a place or a direction. Therefore this wording must be taken in a figurative interpretation (ta'wīl). The meaning is that when a man hears speech while not seeing the speaker, this resembles what happens when one speaks from behind a veil, and resemblance is a cause for the permissibility of metaphor (majāz).

[161]

**Third issue:** The Mu'tazila said: this verse indicates that He, exalted is He, cannot be seen, because He, exalted is He, has restricted the categories of His revelation to these three. If the seeing of Allah were valid, then it would be valid for Allah to speak with the servant at the time the servant sees Him, and then that would be a fourth category beyond these three. Allah, exalted is He, negated the fourth category by His saying ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him﴾, except in these three ways.

The answer: we add a qualifier to the wording, so the implied meaning becomes: "It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him in this world except in one of these three categories." In that case, what you have mentioned does not follow. Although adding this qualifier is contrary to the apparent meaning, it is necessary to resort to it in order to reconcile these verses with the verses indicating that vision will occur on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah knows best.

**Fourth issue:** The community (ummah) has agreed that Allah, exalted is He, is a speaker (mutakallim). Everyone other than the Ash'ariyya and their followers has unanimously held that the speech of Allah is these letters that are heard and these sounds that are composed. As for al-Ash'ari and his followers, they claimed that the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is an eternal attribute (ṣifa qadīma) that is expressed by these letters and sounds.

As for the first group, those who said that the speech of Allah, exalted is He, is these letters and words, they are two groups. One of them is the Hanbalites, who said that these letters are eternal. These people are too base to be mentioned among the intelligent. It happened one day that I said to some of them: If Allah spoke with these letters, He would either speak with them all at once, or in succession and sequence. The first is invalid, because speaking with the whole of these letters at once would not produce this composed arrangement in this sequence and succession. Therefore this composed arrangement of these successive letters would not be the speech of Allah, exalted is He. The second is also invalid, because if He spoke with them in succession and sequence, they would be originated (muḥdatha). When that man heard this argument, he said: "It is obligatory upon us to affirm (nuqirr) and to pass over (namurr)," meaning: we affirm that the Qur'an is eternal, and we pass over this speech according to what we heard. I was astonished at the soundness of that speaker's heart. As for the intelligent people, they have unanimously agreed that these letters and sounds come into existence after not having been, and become present after having been non-existent. Then their expressions differed as to whether they are created (makhlūq), or whether one should not say that, but rather say that they are originated (ḥādith), or express it in another wording. They also differed as to whether these letters subsist in the essence of Allah, exalted is He, or whether He creates them in another body. The first is the view of the Karramiyya, and the second is the view of the Mu'tazila.

As for the Ash'ariyya, who claimed that the speech of Allah is an eternal attribute indicated by these words and expressions, they agreed that His saying ﴿or from behind a veil﴾ means that the angel and the messenger hear that speech, which is exempt from letter and sound, from behind a veil. They said: just as it is not far-fetched that one sees the essence of Allah although He is not a body and not in a space, what is far-fetched about hearing the speech of Allah although it is not a letter and not a sound?

Abu Mansur al-Maturidi al-Samarqandi claimed that this subsisting attribute cannot be heard, and that what is heard is only letters and sounds that Allah, exalted is He, creates in the tree. This view is close to the view of the Mu'tazila. And Allah knows best.

**Fifth issue:** The Qadi said: this verse indicates the origination (ḥudūth) of the speech of Allah, exalted is He, in several respects:

First: His saying ﴿that Allah should speak to him﴾ indicates this, because the word ﴿an﴾ with the imperfect verb conveys the future.

Second: He described the speech as revelation, because the word "revelation" indicates that it occurred in the swiftest manner.

Third: His saying ﴿or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ requires that the speech which the angel conveys to the human messenger be like the speech he heard from Allah. What he conveys to the human messenger is originated. So when the speech he heard from Allah is similar to this which he conveyed to the human messenger, and this which he conveyed to the human messenger is originated, and the like of the originated is originated, it is necessary to say that the speech he heard from Allah is originated.

[162]

Fourth: His saying ﴿or that He sends a messenger and he reveals﴾ requires that the revelation occur after the sending, and whatever's occurrence is subsequent to the occurrence of something else is originated.

The answer: we redirect the whole of these aspects you have mentioned to the letters and sounds, and we acknowledge that they are originated, coming into existence after not having been. The self-evident intellect bears witness that the matter is so. So what need is there to establish this claimed point, whose soundness you know by the self-evident intellect and by the apparent meanings of the Qur'an? And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**Sixth issue:** It has been established that revelation from Allah, exalted is He, either does not occur through another person, and it is impossible that all revelation occurs through another person, for otherwise either an infinite regress (tasalsul) or circularity (dawr) would follow, and both are impossible. Therefore it is necessary to acknowledge that there is a revelation which occurs without another person. Then here are some discussions:

**First discussion:** The first person who heard the revelation of Allah without another person, how does he know that the speech he heard is the speech of Allah? If we say that he heard that eternal attribute, exempt from being a letter and a sound, it is not far-fetched that when he hears it he knows by necessity that it is the speech of Allah, exalted is He, and it is not far-fetched to say that he then needs an additional proof. But if we say that what is heard is the letter and the sound, it is impossible to be certain that it is the speech of Allah, exalted is He, unless a proof appears indicating that this heard thing is the speech of Allah, exalted is He.

**Second discussion:** When the messenger hears it from the angel, how does he know that this conveyor is a sinless angel and not a misguiding devil? The truth is that he cannot be certain of that except on the basis of a miracle (mu'jiza) indicating that this conveyor is a sinless angel and not an evil devil. On this basis, the revelation from Allah, exalted is He, is not completed except through three levels of the appearance of miracles:

The first level: when the angel hears that speech from Allah, exalted is He, there must be a miracle for him indicating that this speech is the speech of Allah, exalted is He.

The second level: when that angel reaches the messenger, there must also be a miracle for him.

The third level: when that messenger conveys it to the community, there must also be a miracle for him. Thus it is established that obligation does not fall upon creation except after the occurrence of three levels of miracles.

**Third discussion:** There is no doubt that an angel among the angels heard the revelation from Allah, exalted is He, at the outset. That angel is Gabriel (Jibril). It may be said: perhaps Gabriel heard it from another angel. All of these are possible, even through a thousand intermediaries, and nothing has been found that indicates certainty about any one of these possibilities.

**Fourth discussion:** Is there anyone among humans who heard the revelation of Allah, exalted is He, without an intermediary? It is well known that Moses, peace be upon him, heard the speech of Allah without an intermediary, based on His saying: ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾. It has also been said that Muhammad (ﷺ) heard it too, based on His saying: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10].

**Fifth discussion:** The angels are able to appear to people in different forms. So supposing that the Messenger (ﷺ) sees him each time, it would be necessary for him to need a miracle, so that he would know that the one he sees this time is the same as the one he saw the first time. And if he does not see his person, then the need for a miracle would be even stronger, because of the possibility that confusion occurred regarding the voice. However, the claim that a miracle must be shown every time has not been held by anyone.

[163]

**Seventh issue:** The disputations mentioned in the Qur'an between Allah, exalted is He, and Iblis indicate that He, exalted is He, was speaking with Iblis without an intermediary. Whether that is called revelation from Allah, exalted is He, to Iblis or not, the more apparent view is that it is not so called. And at this point there must be a complete and subtle discussion.

**The Eighth Issue:** Nafi' recited *"aw yursila rasulan"* (أَوْ يُرْسِلُ رَسُولًا) with a *raf'* (مرفوع) vowel on the *lam*, and *"fa-yuhiya"* (فَيُوحِي) with a sukun on the *ya'*. Its position is in the nominative case, on the assumption of the implied phrase: *"wa-huwa yursilu fa-yuhiya"* (and He sends, so He reveals). The rest of the readers recited it in the accusative (*nasb*), interpreting it as a verbal noun (*ta'wil al-masdar*), as if it were said: *"It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation (wahyan), or by making him hear His speech from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger."* However, there is a difficulty here: the phrase *wahyan aw isma'an* is a noun, while the phrase *"aw yursila"* is a verb, and coordinating a verb with a noun is considered weak. This was answered by saying that the intended meaning is: *"It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except that He reveal to him by revelation (illa an yuhiya ilayhi wahyan), or make him hear by making him hear (aw yusmi'a isma'an) from behind a veil, or send a messenger (aw yursila rasulan)."*

**The Ninth Issue:** According to the People of the Truth (Ahl al-Haqq), the correct view is that while the angel conveys the revelation to the Messenger, Satan cannot cast falsehood into the course of that revelation. Some have said that this is possible, citing the words of Allah the Exalted: *"We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he spoke, Satan cast into his wish"* (22:52). They also said that Satan cast, in the course of Surat al-Najm, *"Those are the exalted cranes, whose intercession is to be hoped for."* Our friend, the king Sam ibn Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, who was the most excellent of the men of authority I ever met, used to say: "This statement, after the strong and overpowering proofs, is false for two other reasons:"

*The first:* The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sees me in a dream has indeed seen me, for Satan cannot take on my form." If Satan cannot take on the form of the Messenger in a dream, how could he be able to imitate Jibril (Gabriel) at the time of conveying the revelation of Allah the Exalted?

*The second:* The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Umar never took a path except that Satan took another path." If Satan cannot be present with Umar on a single path, how could he be able to be present with Jibril at the moment of conveying the revelation of Allah the Exalted?

**The Tenth Issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted, *"so that he reveals by His permission what He wills"* (42:51), mean: that angel reveals, by the permission of Allah, what Allah wills. This implies that goodness is not good because of an attribute that returns to it, and that evil is not evil because of an attribute that returns to it. Rather, Allah may command whatever He wills without specification, and forbid whatever He wills without specification. For if the matter were not so, His saying "what He wills" would not be correct. And Allah knows best.

Then Allah the Exalted said at the end of the verse: *"Indeed He is Most High, All-Wise."* That is, He is exalted above the attributes of the created beings, and *"All-Wise"* means He carries out His acts in accordance with the requirements of wisdom. He speaks at times without an intermediary, by way of inspiration (ilham); at other times by making speech heard; and at a third time through the mediation of the noble angels. When Allah the Exalted explained the modes of revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them, He said: *"And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command"* (42:52). The intended meaning is the Qur'an, and He called it a *"spirit"* (ruh) because it gives life after the death of ignorance or disbelief.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: *"You did not know what the Book was, nor faith"* (42:52). The scholars differed concerning this verse, with a consensus (ijma') that it is not permissible to say that the messengers were upon disbelief before revelation. They mentioned several answers:

*First:* *"You did not know what the Book was"*, that is, the Qur'an, *"nor faith"*, that is, the prayer (salah), based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: *"And Allah would not let your faith go to waste"* (2:143), meaning your prayer. [Page 164]

*Second:* This is to be understood as an elision of a noun (hadhf al-mudaf). That is: *"You did not know what the Book was, nor who the people of faith were"*, meaning who believes and who does not believe.

*Third:* *"You did not know what the Book was, nor faith"* when you were a child in the cradle.

*Fourth:* "Faith" (iman) is an expression for affirming everything that Allah the Exalted has obligated. Before prophethood, he (ﷺ) was not acquainted with all of Allah's obligations, but he was acquainted with Allah the Exalted, and this does not contradict what we have mentioned.

*Fifth:* The attributes of Allah the Exalted are of two kinds. Some of them can be known by purely rational proofs, and others cannot be known except through revealed (sam'i) proofs. This second kind had not been known to him before prophethood.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: *"But We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* (42:52). They differed regarding the pronoun in His saying *"But We made it"*. Some said it refers to the Qur'an alone, not to faith, because it is by it that rulings are known; therefore it is rightly likened to the light by which one is guided. Others said it refers to both together, and this is acceptable because their meaning is one, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: *"And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush to it"* (62:11).

* * *

Then He said: *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants."* This indicates that, after He made the Qur'an itself a guidance in its own essence, as He said: *"guidance for the righteous"* (2:2), He may guide some by it and not others. And this guidance is nothing other than an expression for the call (da'wah) and the clarification of the proofs. For Allah the Exalted said of Muhammad (ﷺ): *"And indeed, you guide to a straight path"* (42:52), which conveys generality with respect to all. His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* conveys particularity. Thus it is established that guidance in the sense of the call is general, while the guidance in His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* is specific. The specific guidance is other than the general guidance. Therefore, what is meant by His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* must be something different from the manifestation of the proofs and the removal of excuses. Then Allah the Exalted said to Muhammad (ﷺ): *"And indeed, you guide to a straight path"* (42:52). He thus made clear that just as the Qur'an guides, so too the Messenger guides. By this He draws attention to the fact that the One who is worthy of worship is the One who owns the heavens and the earth. The purpose of this is to invalidate the claim of those who worship other than Allah.

* * *

Then He said: *"Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned"* (42:53). This is in the manner of a warning and a rebuke. He made clear that the affair of whoever does not accept these obligations returns to Allah the Exalted, that is, to where there is no judge other than Him, and He will recompense each of them with what they deserve of reward or punishment.

He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The commentary on this surah was completed on the last day of Friday, the eighth of the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, in the year six hundred and three. O Director of affairs, O Eternal Ruler of the ages, O Giver of every good and joy, O Repeller of trials and evils, bring us to the abodes of light, in the darkness of the graves, by Your grace and mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful.
