Third: His saying ﴿or that He sends a messenger and he reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ requires that the speech which the angel conveys to the human messenger be like the speech he heard from Allah. What he conveys to the human messenger is originated. So when the speech he heard from Allah is similar to this which he conveyed to the human messenger, and this which he conveyed to the human messenger is originated, and the like of the originated is originated, it is necessary to say that the speech he heard from Allah is originated.

[162]

Fourth: His saying ﴿or that He sends a messenger and he reveals﴾ requires that the revelation occur after the sending, and whatever's occurrence is subsequent to the occurrence of something else is originated.

The answer: we redirect the whole of these aspects you have mentioned to the letters and sounds, and we acknowledge that they are originated, coming into existence after not having been. The self-evident intellect bears witness that the matter is so. So what need is there to establish this claimed point, whose soundness you know by the self-evident intellect and by the apparent meanings of the Qur'an? And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**Sixth issue:** It has been established that revelation from Allah, exalted is He, either does not occur through another person, and it is impossible that all revelation occurs through another person, for otherwise either an infinite regress (tasalsul) or circularity (dawr) would follow, and both are impossible. Therefore it is necessary to acknowledge that there is a revelation which occurs without another person. Then here are some discussions:

**First discussion:** The first person who heard the revelation of Allah without another person, how does he know that the speech he heard is the speech of Allah? If we say that he heard that eternal attribute, exempt from being a letter and a sound, it is not far-fetched that when he hears it he knows by necessity that it is the speech of Allah, exalted is He, and it is not far-fetched to say that he then needs an additional proof. But if we say that what is heard is the letter and the sound, it is impossible to be certain that it is the speech of Allah, exalted is He, unless a proof appears indicating that this heard thing is the speech of Allah, exalted is He.

**Second discussion:** When the messenger hears it from the angel, how does he know that this conveyor is a sinless angel and not a misguiding devil? The truth is that he cannot be certain of that except on the basis of a miracle (mu'jiza) indicating that this conveyor is a sinless angel and not an evil devil. On this basis, the revelation from Allah, exalted is He, is not completed except through three levels of the appearance of miracles:

The first level: when the angel hears that speech from Allah, exalted is He, there must be a miracle for him indicating that this speech is the speech of Allah, exalted is He.

The second level: when that angel reaches the messenger, there must also be a miracle for him.

The third level: when that messenger conveys it to the community, there must also be a miracle for him. Thus it is established that obligation does not fall upon creation except after the occurrence of three levels of miracles.

**Third discussion:** There is no doubt that an angel among the angels heard the revelation from Allah, exalted is He, at the outset. That angel is Gabriel (Jibril). It may be said: perhaps Gabriel heard it from another angel. All of these are possible, even through a thousand intermediaries, and nothing has been found that indicates certainty about any one of these possibilities.

**Fourth discussion:** Is there anyone among humans who heard the revelation of Allah, exalted is He, without an intermediary? It is well known that Moses, peace be upon him, heard the speech of Allah without an intermediary, based on His saying: ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾. It has also been said that Muhammad (ﷺ) heard it too, based on His saying: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10].

**Fifth discussion:** The angels are able to appear to people in different forms. So supposing that the Messenger (ﷺ) sees him each time, it would be necessary for him to need a miracle, so that he would know that the one he sees this time is the same as the one he saw the first time. And if he does not see his person, then the need for a miracle would be even stronger, because of the possibility that confusion occurred regarding the voice. However, the claim that a miracle must be shown every time has not been held by anyone.

[163]

**Seventh issue:** The disputations mentioned in the Qur'an between Allah, exalted is He, and Iblis indicate that He, exalted is He, was speaking with Iblis without an intermediary. Whether that is called revelation from Allah, exalted is He, to Iblis or not, the more apparent view is that it is not so called. And at this point there must be a complete and subtle discussion.

**The Eighth Issue:** Nafi' recited *"aw yursila rasulan"* (أَوْ يُرْسِلُ رَسُولًا) with a *raf'* (مرفوع) vowel on the *lam*, and *"fa-yuhiya"* (فَيُوحِي) with a sukun on the *ya'*. Its position is in the nominative case, on the assumption of the implied phrase: *"wa-huwa yursilu fa-yuhiya"* (and He sends, so He reveals). The rest of the readers recited it in the accusative (*nasb*), interpreting it as a verbal noun (*ta'wil al-masdar*), as if it were said: *"It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation (wahyan), or by making him hear His speech from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger."* However, there is a difficulty here: the phrase *wahyan aw isma'an* is a noun, while the phrase *"aw yursila"* is a verb, and coordinating a verb with a noun is considered weak. This was answered by saying that the intended meaning is: *"It is not for any human that Allah should speak to him except that He reveal to him by revelation (illa an yuhiya ilayhi wahyan), or make him hear by making him hear (aw yusmi'a isma'an) from behind a veil, or send a messenger (aw yursila rasulan)."*

**The Ninth Issue:** According to the People of the Truth (Ahl al-Haqq), the correct view is that while the angel conveys the revelation to the Messenger, Satan cannot cast falsehood into the course of that revelation. Some have said that this is possible, citing the words of Allah the Exalted: *"We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he spoke, Satan cast into his wish"* (22:52). They also said that Satan cast, in the course of Surat al-Najm, *"Those are the exalted cranes, whose intercession is to be hoped for."* Our friend, the king Sam ibn Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, who was the most excellent of the men of authority I ever met, used to say: "This statement, after the strong and overpowering proofs, is false for two other reasons:"

*The first:* The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sees me in a dream has indeed seen me, for Satan cannot take on my form." If Satan cannot take on the form of the Messenger in a dream, how could he be able to imitate Jibril (Gabriel) at the time of conveying the revelation of Allah the Exalted?

*The second:* The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Umar never took a path except that Satan took another path." If Satan cannot be present with Umar on a single path, how could he be able to be present with Jibril at the moment of conveying the revelation of Allah the Exalted?

**The Tenth Issue:** The words of Allah the Exalted, *"so that he reveals by His permission what He wills"* (42:51), mean: that angel reveals, by the permission of Allah, what Allah wills. This implies that goodness is not good because of an attribute that returns to it, and that evil is not evil because of an attribute that returns to it. Rather, Allah may command whatever He wills without specification, and forbid whatever He wills without specification. For if the matter were not so, His saying "what He wills" would not be correct. And Allah knows best.

Then Allah the Exalted said at the end of the verse: *"Indeed He is Most High, All-Wise."* That is, He is exalted above the attributes of the created beings, and *"All-Wise"* means He carries out His acts in accordance with the requirements of wisdom. He speaks at times without an intermediary, by way of inspiration (ilham); at other times by making speech heard; and at a third time through the mediation of the noble angels. When Allah the Exalted explained the modes of revelation to the prophets, peace be upon them, He said: *"And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command"* (42:52). The intended meaning is the Qur'an, and He called it a *"spirit"* (ruh) because it gives life after the death of ignorance or disbelief.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: *"You did not know what the Book was, nor faith"* (42:52). The scholars differed concerning this verse, with a consensus (ijma') that it is not permissible to say that the messengers were upon disbelief before revelation. They mentioned several answers:

*First:* *"You did not know what the Book was"*, that is, the Qur'an, *"nor faith"*, that is, the prayer (salah), based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: *"And Allah would not let your faith go to waste"* (2:143), meaning your prayer. [Page 164]

*Second:* This is to be understood as an elision of a noun (hadhf al-mudaf). That is: *"You did not know what the Book was, nor who the people of faith were"*, meaning who believes and who does not believe.

*Third:* *"You did not know what the Book was, nor faith"* when you were a child in the cradle.

*Fourth:* "Faith" (iman) is an expression for affirming everything that Allah the Exalted has obligated. Before prophethood, he (ﷺ) was not acquainted with all of Allah's obligations, but he was acquainted with Allah the Exalted, and this does not contradict what we have mentioned.

*Fifth:* The attributes of Allah the Exalted are of two kinds. Some of them can be known by purely rational proofs, and others cannot be known except through revealed (sam'i) proofs. This second kind had not been known to him before prophethood.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: *"But We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* (42:52). They differed regarding the pronoun in His saying *"But We made it"*. Some said it refers to the Qur'an alone, not to faith, because it is by it that rulings are known; therefore it is rightly likened to the light by which one is guided. Others said it refers to both together, and this is acceptable because their meaning is one, like the saying of Allah the Exalted: *"And when they see a trade or a diversion, they rush to it"* (62:11).

* * *

Then He said: *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants."* This indicates that, after He made the Qur'an itself a guidance in its own essence, as He said: *"guidance for the righteous"* (2:2), He may guide some by it and not others. And this guidance is nothing other than an expression for the call (da'wah) and the clarification of the proofs. For Allah the Exalted said of Muhammad (ﷺ): *"And indeed, you guide to a straight path"* (42:52), which conveys generality with respect to all. His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* conveys particularity. Thus it is established that guidance in the sense of the call is general, while the guidance in His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* is specific. The specific guidance is other than the general guidance. Therefore, what is meant by His saying *"by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"* must be something different from the manifestation of the proofs and the removal of excuses. It is also not permissible that it be an expression for guidance to the path of Paradise, because He said: *"But We made it a light by which We guide whom We will of Our servants"*, that is, We made the Qur'an a light by which We guide whom We will. This befits only the guidance that occurs in this world. Furthermore, guidance to Paradise, according to you, is obligatory for some and forbidden for others, and on either assumption, His saying *"whom We will of Our servants"* would serve no purpose. Thus it is established that what is meant is that He guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills, and there is no objection to Him in this.

Then Allah the Exalted said to Muhammad (ﷺ): *"And indeed, you guide to a straight path"* (42:52). He thus made clear that just as the Qur'an guides, so too the Messenger guides. And He made clear that he guides *"to a straight path"*, and He explained that this path is *"the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth"* (42:53). By this He draws attention to the fact that the One who is worthy of worship is the One who owns the heavens and the earth. The purpose of this is to invalidate the claim of those who worship other than Allah.

* * *

Then He said: *"Unquestionably, to Allah all matters are returned"* (42:53). This is in the manner of a warning and a rebuke. He made clear that the affair of whoever does not accept these obligations returns to Allah the Exalted, that is, to where there is no judge other than Him, and He will recompense each of them with what they deserve of reward or punishment.

He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The commentary on this surah was completed on the last day of Friday, the eighth of the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, in the year six hundred and three. O Director of affairs, O Eternal Ruler of the ages, O Giver of every good and joy, O Repeller of trials and evils, bring us to the abodes of light, in the darkness of the graves, by Your grace and mercy, O Most Merciful of the merciful.
